**Verdict: KNOWN, with medium confidence.** The behaviour is locally phase-locked patches with low global order and few vortices. It matches the established picture of a locally coupled Kuramoto lattice behaving like the 2D XY model.

**1. Model family.** The rules describe phase oscillators on a lattice with local (neighbour) sinusoidal coupling. `C.KURA(K=0.2)` is a plain Kuramoto lattice. `PHASE_COUPLE(K, p)` looks like the same coupling applied stochastically, so each oscillator updates with probability p per step. I could not verify this reading of the rule grammar. Because of that, I treat the stochastic update as a possible variant, not part of the core model.

**2. Reading the observed features.**
- Local order is very high (p_local_r = 0.973) and global order is low (p_r = 0.119). The frequency spread is near zero and vortex density is very low.
- Together these point to a frequency-locked, locally phase-coherent state. Its coherent domains or smooth phase gradients have different phases, so the global r stays small. Few vortices remain.
- This is the standard outcome of a short-range Kuramoto lattice with identical or weakly disordered frequencies.

**3. What the literature says** (all found in the searches and read in the returned text):
- **Equivalence to the XY model.** The Kuramoto order parameter equals the XY model's absolute global magnetisation. Synchronising from an incoherent start is therefore the same as relaxing the XY model after a quench to T=0 (Levis, Pagonabarraga & Diaz-Guilera, arXiv 1608.02423).
- **No long-range order in 2D.** Short-range 2D XY or Kuramoto systems lack long-range order because of spin-wave fluctuations and topological defects (Mermin–Wagner). This is described in the spin-torque-oscillator Kuramoto paper (Sci. Rep. srep32528, arXiv 1604.01927).
- **Coarsening in the noisy Kuramoto lattice.** With zero intrinsic frequency, the 2D Kuramoto lattice is equivalent to the 2D XY model with non-conserved dynamics. It keeps XY-like coarsening, with correlation length growing as t/log t and vortex density decaying as log t/t. Vortices diffuse, interact and annihilate (Frontiers in Physics 2022, 10.3389/fphy.2022.976515; arXiv 2206.11730).
- **Local coherence without global coherence.** The Kuramoto review (Acebrón et al., "The Kuramoto model: a simple paradigm…") separates global synchronisation from phase locking or partial synchronisation in short-range lattices. It notes global sync is rarely seen except as K and N go to infinity. Another source says the frequencies of many oscillators can sync while the phases stay spread out (MIT 8.334 project note). A local 1D Kuramoto paper likewise notes that frequency synchronisation can occur without phase coherence, with r≈0.
- **Earliest sources for the underlying XY coarsening.** These are cited in the reference list of arXiv 2206.11730: Yurke et al., Phys. Rev. E 47, 1525 (1993); Rojas & Rutenberg, PRE 60, 212 (1999); and Bray's review, Adv. Phys. 51, 481 (2002). I only saw these as reference entries, not their text, so I haven't checked their content.
- **Review.** Bray's "Theory of phase-ordering kinetics" is the review for coarsening. Acebrón et al. is the review for Kuramoto on lattices.

**4. What differs (the possible variant).**
- The probabilistic update (p = 0.03 to 0.1) is random sequential or asynchronous updating. It mostly sets the effective time scale and a little extra noise.
- For the gradient-like, identical-frequency case, this probably doesn't change the phase-ordering class. I did not find a paper that studies p-gated Kuramoto updates specifically.
- That gap could matter if p-gating changes defect dynamics or the fraction of vortices frozen in. I didn't search for it directly, so I don't call it LITERATURE-SILENT.

**5. Confidence.** Medium. The behaviour (local locking, low global r, few vortices) is well covered by the XY and Kuramoto lattice literature. I couldn't confirm the rule semantics, whether the frequencies are identical, or the lattice size. I also didn't read the earliest coarsening papers directly.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** The behaviour is described in the literature. I'm only partly sure about how it applies to the "non-textbook fingerprint".

**1. Model family**
- The core rule is a synchronous, deterministic majority-vote cellular automaton. It has 3 states, a Moore (8-neighbour) neighbourhood and periodic boundaries.
- The cells are labelled in the Potts sense, so it is the zero-temperature 3-state Potts / voter-style "majority rule" model with parallel updating.
- The listed "same class" members are different systems (a 2-type cyclic rule, and a 3-type rule with a diffusing field plus majority). I did not search these separately. The majority component is the one that matches the coarsening claim.

**2. The specific behaviour**
- **Coarsening that stalls into frozen or stripe-like domains.** The observed pattern is a few large, spatially correlated domains (corrlen 13.5, n_domains about 1.6, Moran I 0.935). It passes the coarsening test but does not look like clean textbook coarsening.
  - Zero-temperature coarsening of the 2D 3-state Potts model on a square lattice does not always reach the ground state. Both ground states and complicated static states are reached with non-zero probabilities. The system may also wander ad infinitum on an iso-energy subspace of blinker states. (Redner and co-authors, J. Stat. Mech. 2013.)
  - A review-style source notes that on the square lattice with q=3 the ground-state probability is only about 0.1, and the most common final states are "frozen" configurations with two or more surviving spin states. The same source says the existence of non-ground final states was realised in the Potts model before the equivalent finding in the Ising model. (This is the "High-degeneracy Potts coarsening" arXiv paper, 2101.02425.)
  - For the Ising case, a 2D ferromagnet quenched to zero temperature converges to either a ground state or an infinitely long-lived metastable stripe state (Barros, Krapivsky and Redner, arXiv 0905.3521). Cond-mat/0105037 reports that the system first relaxes to a metastable stripe state with probability ≈1/3.
- **Majority rule specifically.** Redner and co-authors' "Majority Rule Dynamics in Finite Dimensions" (cond-mat/0408219) describes spatially coherent, long-lived states of relatively flat stripes in two dimensions that spontaneously break the isotropy of the rule. This is the closest match to a high-correlation-length, low-domain-count state.
- **Moore-neighbourhood, synchronous majority CA.**
  - Bagnoli and Mencarelli (arXiv 2604.10082, April 2026) treat 2D totalistic majority CA with a variable interaction range. They report that at density 0.5 the dynamics is dominated by a coarsening process, which stops when clusters with a definite curvature radius are established. This is a binary model, and it is a preprint.
  - For the synchronous dynamics, Goles and Olivos (1980) proved that the repeated application of such symmetric threshold maps leads either to a fixed point or to a cycle of length two.
  - Goles and Tchuente (1983) extended this to an arbitrary number of opinions, so it covers 3 states. I did not read that paper directly. I only saw it cited in an IJCAI paper.
  - So the long-time state of this rule is either frozen or flips with period 2. That could help explain the odd activity trend and reversals (g_reversals 0.89), but I haven't checked this against the simulation.

**3. Differences from the textbook case (KNOWN-VARIANT considerations)**
- The textbook Potts/Ising results use asynchronous Glauber dynamics on a 4-neighbour lattice. This system is synchronous with 8 neighbours and 3 states.
- These differences change the details: the types of frozen states, the blinker or period-2 behaviour, and the curvature stalling. They do not change the mechanism. Majority-driven coarsening is curvature-driven, and it stalls on stripes or blocks, or on clusters with a fixed curvature radius.
- I did not find a paper that characterises the exact 3-state synchronous Moore-8 case with this particular set of metrics. A short search found no such source. I judge that this is unlikely to matter, because the mechanism is the same as in the sources above.
- The 5622 rule programs and the other class members (cyclic and diffusion-coupled rules) were not checked for extra behaviour beyond majority coarsening. If the other members really differ, that part is unverified.

**4. Confidence: medium-high**
- High that the mechanism (majority and zero-temperature Potts coarsening that stalls) and the general fixed-point or 2-cycle result are documented.
- Medium that there is nothing novel in the exact synchronous 3-state Moore variant. I did not find a paper on that exact variant, and I did not read the Goles–Tchuente paper directly.

**1. Model family.** This is an adaptive (co-evolving) network with homophilic "rewire-to-same" dynamics. A node cuts a link to a different-state neighbour and reconnects to a random node of its own state. Here the node types (states) never change. The other rules in the class (kN=3 or 4, REWIRE p=0.1, 0.3 or 1.0) look like the same rewiring at different mean degree and rewiring probability.

**2. Where the behaviour is reported.**
- **Earliest clear source: Holme & Newman, Phys. Rev. E 74, 056108 (2006).** I could not read the paper itself. I confirmed it through secondary sources.
  - A statistical-physics review describes their model: with probability 1−φ a node adopts its neighbour's opinion, and with probability φ it rewires the link to a new vertex chosen at random among those with its own opinion.
  - The same review says that in the limit φ→1, rewiring will quickly split the network into disconnected components that separately reach a different consensus state.
  - It credits Holme & Newman with the first report of this type of transition: "Such type of transition was first reported in (Holme and Newman, 2006)".
- **Review: Gross & Blasius, J. R. Soc. Interface 5, 259 (2008).** Its opinion-formation section covers the Holme–Newman model. It describes a final state in which the network is decomposed into disconnected components, each of uniform opinion. Kozma & Barrat (PRE 77, 016102) make the same point: each opinion cluster corresponds to a distinct connected component in the final configuration. I read these only as search snippets, not full texts.
- **Closest match to your system: arXiv 2511.15043, "Structural transitions induced by adaptive rewiring in networks with fixed states."** It studies adaptive networks where node states remain fixed and only the connections evolve via state-dependent rewiring.
  - It reports three phases: random connectivity, community structure, and fragmentation.
  - It finds that community structure emerges only under moderate homophily, while extreme homophily or heterophily lead to fragmentation or random networks.
  - It uses modularity-based order parameters, which matches the high type-modularity (0.663) in your fingerprint.
  - I only saw the abstract and snippets, and it is a recent preprint.
- **Related: Henry, Prałat & Zhang, PNAS 108, 8605 (2011).** This is Schelling-style network segregation with fixed attributes. It finds that segregated networks always emerge regardless of the level of aversion. Another paper describes the model as stubborn individuals with fixed opinions who tend to rewire their ties to those with similar opinions.

**3. What differs from the textbook case, and whether it matters.**
- **No opinion-copying.** Types are frozen, so this is the φ→1 limit of Holme–Newman, not the transition region. There is no consensus phase and no critical slowing down. It is just a forced split into same-type clusters.
- **Why the fingerprint looks unusual.** With a fixed number of types, the components are bounded below by the number of types (3 here), plus any stranded nodes. That explains the high n_components, the high type-modularity and the entropy. Edge turnover is a transient: once no cross-type links remain, the system is frozen. This is my inference from the rule, not something I found in a source.
- **Rule differences.** I treated "applied every step" and the REWIRE(p) variants as rewiring probabilities. That fits the p-parameterised class in the literature. Mean degree 3–4 is also standard. None of these changes the qualitative result.
- **Not checked.** I did not look for a specific source on the degree-CV rise (0.412) or the negative cyclic-changes feature. Both look like side effects of the same process, but I have no citation for them.

**4. Confidence: medium-high.** The mechanism and the fragmentation outcome are well documented in several independent sources. The fixed-state version has a dedicated, very recent paper, which I read only as an abstract. I did not find a source that explains the secondary metrics (edge turnover, cyclic changes, degree CV), but I see no reason to expect anything novel there.

**1. Model family**
- It is a Schelling-type residential segregation model. This is a lattice with vacancies and a Moore (8-neighbour) neighbourhood.
- An agent whose same-type share of occupied neighbours is below a threshold θ relocates to a random empty cell.
- Your system has 3 types plus a vacancy state, random initial conditions and periodic boundaries.
- The "CF … fields=1 D=[…]" prefix suggests a diffusing field. The rule you described never uses it, so I assume it doesn't affect this behaviour.

**2. Earliest source and reviews**
- **Earliest source.** Schelling's "Dynamic models of segregation" appeared in the *Journal of Mathematical Sociology* 1:143–186 in 1971. Its simulation model has members of two recognizable groups distribute themselves in neighborhoods defined by reference to their own locations. It used a 3×3 Moore neighbourhood. Schelling (1971) employed a 3 × 3 Moore neighborhood.
- **Physics treatment (closest to your setup).** Gauvin, Vannimenus and Nadal, "Phase diagram of a Schelling segregation model" (*Eur. Phys. J. B* 70:293, 2009). Its variant has tolerance and the density of vacant sites as the basic variables. It reports segregated, mixed and "frozen" regimes separated by sharp transitions. A secondary description says high tolerance (S < 0.25) gives no segregation, and between the extremes the model gives segregated states where homogeneous communities adjoin one another. That is the regime of your θ=0.2 run.
- **Review.** Grauwin et al., "Dynamic models of residential segregation: brief review…" (arXiv 0907.1777). Its abstract restates Schelling's result that a small preference for same-colour neighbours can lead to total segregation.
- **Random relocation to a vacancy.** This is the standard textbook version. Agents below the satisfaction threshold relocate at random into a vacant location.
- **More than two groups.** Multi-group versions are routine. One simulator I found offers a 3-group mode, though that is not a primary source. Schelling's 1971 paper itself used two groups.
- **Analytic and scaling work.** I saw these only as reference-list entries in my results, so I did not read them: Immorlica et al. (exponential segregation with tolerant agents) and the "Self-organized Segregation on the Grid" paper (arXiv 1705.08586).

**3. Why the fingerprint looks non-textbook**
I'm inferring this, not reading it from a source.
- With 3 types plus about 25% vacancies, a random configuration already has a same-type share near 1/3 among occupied neighbours.
- At θ=0.2 only a minority of agents are initially unhappy. This matches the "no or weak segregation at high tolerance" regime in the literature.
- That would explain a correlation length of 1.0, a domain count of about 7, and a small negative activity trend. These suggest few agents move and the system quickly freezes into a mostly random pattern.
- The max entropy of 1.0 and n_types of 3.0 just reflect that all three types persist. They are not signs of a new effect.
- Your "standard test" passes only marginally at low θ, so it is reasonable that the fingerprint doesn't look like a textbook segregated state.
- The thresholds in your class (0.2–0.5) span the known tolerance range. The θ=0.3–0.5 runs should look more like textbook segregation.

**4. Differences that probably don't matter**
- Your update is probably parallel or synchronous with random-empty-cell moves. Schelling used sequential moves, and Gauvin et al. used a random-agent update. These change the transient dynamics and not the qualitative regimes.
- Moves are not conditioned on the target being satisfactory. That is the standard "random relocation" variant.
- Three groups instead of two is a known extension.
- I did not find a source that specifically describes the 3-group, θ=0.2, 25%-vacancy statistics.

**5. Confidence: high.**
- This is a canonical model, and the behaviour (tolerance-dependent segregation and a mixed or frozen regime) is documented in a primary source and a physics-style analysis.
- The remaining uncertainty is the exact 3-type fingerprint. I treat it as a parameter regime of a known model and did not search for it specifically.

- **Identical oscillators on Erdős–Rényi graphs are well studied.** Kassabov, Strogatz and Townsend's "A global synchronization theorem for oscillators on a random graph" (Chaos 2022) studies n identical Kuramoto oscillators on Erdős–Rényi graphs with unit-strength bidirectional coupling. The paper asks whether there is a connectivity threshold for global synchrony.
- **Sparse graphs near the connectivity threshold are covered.** Expander-graph work (arXiv 2210.12788) shows that for p ⩾ (1+ε)(log n)/n, the homogeneous Kuramoto model on G(n,p) globally synchronizes with probability tending to one. Jain–Mizgerd–Sawhney show that the random graph process becomes globally synchronizing as soon as it is connected, and that connectivity is necessary.
- **Your graph is below that threshold.** At N=200 and mean degree 4, log(n)/n ≈ 0.027, while p ≈ 0.02. So the graph is typically disconnected, with isolated nodes and small components. Connectivity is necessary for global synchrony, so full r=1 is not guaranteed.
- **Competing stable states are also documented.** Some graphs have other stable equilibria, such as twisted states, in addition to the synchronized state. Graphs with a cyclic clustering or a long induced subpath can have a non-synchronous stable phase-locked solution. That paper is Sparse networks of identical Kuramoto oscillators (Physica A).
- **Reviews.** Arenas, Díaz-Guilera, Kurths, Moreno and Zhou, "Synchronization in complex networks" (Phys. Rep. 469, 2008), is on the cosnet.bifi.es and arXiv 0805.2976 results. Acebrón et al., "The Kuramoto model: a simple paradigm for synchronization phenomena" (Rev. Mod. Phys. 2005), describes partial synchronization with 0<r<1. Rodrigues et al., "The Kuramoto model in complex networks" (Phys. Rep. 2016), appears only in reference lists in my results.
- **Earliest source.** The model itself is Kuramoto (1975), which appears in a reference list in the results. I did not find a source in the results for the earliest identical-oscillator-on-a-random-graph result, so I'm not claiming one.

**Why r≈0.87 and not 1 (my interpretation, not verified).** The most likely explanation is that each connected component locks internally. Isolated nodes and small components are common in a graph this sparse. With identical frequencies and no coupling between components, the components stay at different offsets. That gives a stable r<1 with low r variance and low frequency spread. Twisted-state-like or locked non-synchronous states are an alternative. Both are consistent with the literature above, but I did not find a paper that reports r≈0.87 for this exact setup.

- p=0.1 is probably just slower stochastic updating. The final locked state is the same, but I found no paper on that exact update scheme.
- K=0.1, 0.3 and 1.0 only change the timescale for identical oscillators.
- The repeated KURA rule (applied twice) probably just rescales the effective coupling.

None of these likely changes the qualitative outcome.

- **Earliest clear source.** Strogatz & Mirollo, "Phase locking and critical phenomena in lattices of coupled nonlinear oscillators". **Verdict: KNOWN.** I disagree with the first pass's "KNOWN-VARIANT". Nothing in the reported numbers points to behaviour the literature doesn't already cover.

**1. This exact rule is a well-known, named rule.** Three colours, Moore neighbourhood, range 1, threshold 3 is "313" (R1/T3/C3/NM) in Mirek Wójtowicz's MCell catalogue. It is credited to David Griffeath and described as "the only three-color rule in the range-1 CCA rulespace that exhibits significant self-organization." It sports a number of distinct spiral types. So the textbook behaviour for this rule is spiral waves, not coarsening.

**2. The first pass picked the wrong reference phase.** The metastable "turbulent" phase it cited comes from Shalizi et al., whose figures use 4 colours. In that setting, at T=3 one finds "turbulence," which is metastable: spiral waves can form and take over the whole grid, but on finite lattices this doesn't always happen, and the turbulent phase can last a very long time. That describes the 4-colour rule (R1/T3/C4), not this 3-colour one. The overall phase picture still applies, though: at high thresholds you get static solid blocks (fixation); at intermediate thresholds, wave fronts form, travel for a while, then break up.

**3. Making the update random (p = 0.1) isn't a new twist either.** The founding paper on these automata already says that, started from random states, they typically nucleate locally periodic 'ram's horns' or spirals, and that the corresponding random processes produce 'forest fire' equilibria with large-scale stochastic wave fronts. Random versions were in the programme from the start. Bramson and Griffeath's cyclic particle systems are the continuous-time random counterpart: continuous-time Markov processes with stochastic rather than deterministic evolution. Rock-paper-scissors lattice models also cover the domain behaviour. In 1D, domains grow algebraically over time, while in 2D domains can break up, allowing long-term coexistence. That fits what you saw: all 3 types survive (entropy ≈ 1.0) and there are about 4 domains rather than one winner.

**4. Why the fingerprint doesn't look like textbook coarsening.** Correlation length ≈ 4.7 on a 64×64 grid, Moran's I ≈ 0.77, and about half of all changes being cyclic steps add up to noisy, patchy wave fronts that keep cycling. That is the stochastic-wave-front regime above, not coarsening that settles down. Passing the coarsening test is most likely a labelling side effect: it is a 3-colour rule that makes local patches. The same class also contains noisy-majority rules (p = 0.001), which really do coarsen. So the class merges two different known mechanisms that just look alike on these summary statistics.

**Genuine or artifact?** The pattern itself is real and well documented (excitable-media self-organisation). The "domain coarsening" label is the shaky part. One limit: I didn't find a paper giving this exact asynchronous T=3, 3-colour parameter set, but by your own criterion that's a rule-tuple gap, not a new behaviour. I also didn't read the 1991 papers in full.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** I'm downgrading the first pass's KNOWN-VARIANT. The behaviour is partial (but phase-locked) Kuramoto synchronization on an annealed or fast-switching network. The fast-switching theory and standard Kuramoto locking theory together cover it. The things that made the first pass hedge (discrete time, coupling applied at random, the grammar wording) are details of how the model is built, not a different behaviour.

**What the fingerprint shows.** r ≈ 0.65 with small fluctuation (std 0.057), and almost no spread in effective frequencies (0.025). So the oscillators share one frequency but keep fixed phase offsets that don't close up. That is not textbook full synchrony, which is probably why the pattern-matcher flagged it. But it is a standard state.

**Why this is known:**
1. **Locked frequencies with phases still spread out is the normal Kuramoto picture.** Past a first critical coupling, some oscillators enter a partially phase locked state and their phases evolve with the same time-averaged frequency. In a phase-locked state, the order parameter does not have to be 1. It has been shown to have a strictly positive lower bound (r ⩾ 1/2). So r ≈ 0.65 with matching frequencies is what you'd expect just above the locking threshold. Phases spread out with fixed gaps is exactly what a locked state looks like.
2. **Rewiring every step, so that a sparse graph acts like a mean-field one, is documented.** One study finds sufficiently fast network rewiring can overcome the effects of low network connectivity, inducing partial synchronization on the network. Synchronization can happen for arbitrarily small net connectivity (i.e., for a sparse and infrequent coupling among the oscillators), provided sufficiently fast switching and strong couplings are considered. In the fast-switching limit, the synchronization dynamics is fully captured by the time-averaged connectivity matrix. The transition is still in the usual Kuramoto model class. Similarly, the blinking network considered in [4] was shown to support synchrony if the blinking is fast enough.
3. **The other rules in the class are the same mechanism.** REWIRE(p=1.0) with KURA on kN=2 or kN=4 is an annealed random graph. PHASE_COUPLE at p=0.02–0.1 with one random partner is "blinking" coupling with a low duty cycle, which works like a weaker average coupling. 162 programs giving the same fingerprint is what you'd expect if the averaged network decides the outcome.

**Artifact check:**
- **COPY_RAND inflates r.** The programs that copy a random node's phase push phases together through imitation, not coupling. In those programs some of the 0.65 is caused by the rule itself, which is trivial. It still sits inside the same class.
- **The low frequency spread may be partly measurement.** If effective frequency is averaged over a window, noisy random kicks can make frequencies look more alike than they are.
- **Otherwise it's a genuine emergent state.** For the pure KURA+REWIRE and PHASE_COUPLE programs, a stable, partially coherent locked state comes out of the collective dynamics. It's real, just well known.

**What is not accounted for:** nothing at the level of behaviour. The only open item is that I couldn't find these exact discrete-time "blink with probability p" rules in the literature. Per your criterion, that's not a discovery.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** The system is the voter model on a periodic 2D lattice with a Moore (8-neighbour) neighbourhood, and the behaviour is slow domain coarsening.

**1. Model family**
- The base rule is "copy a random neighbour at rate 0.005, with 2 types". That is the two-state voter model, also called the Clifford–Sudbury or Holley–Liggett model.
- The voter model was introduced independently by Clifford and Sudbury (1973) and Holley and Liggett (1975).
- The "CF … D=[0.2]" variants add a diffusing field to the same copy rule. The rule text gives no coupling between the field and the cell types, so I assume it is irrelevant. I could not check this.
- The `C.MAJ(p=0.001)` variants are different. Majority-rule updating is zero-temperature Glauber/Ising-like dynamics, discussed under variants below.

**2. The specific behaviour: coarsening with slowly decaying interface density**
- **Earliest clear source:** Cox & Griffeath, "Diffusive clustering in the two dimensional voter model", Ann. Probab. 14, 347–370 (1986). The search confirmed the bibliographic record and its follow-up papers.
  - The abstract snippet I could read is only a general description of simulation results and a survey of known results for the voter model.
  - The result that clusters grow diffusively in 2D, with a largest solid-colour square of size about √t, comes from the follow-up. The Bramson–Cox–Griffeath abstract describes a limit law concerning the size of the largest square centered at the origin which is of solid color at a large time t.
  - Durrett's text also notes that Cox and Griffeath (1986) have proved a number of interesting result about clustering in the two dimensional case, which is the "critical dimension."
- **Physics-literature source:** Frachebourg & Krapivsky, Phys. Rev. E 53, R3009 (1996). I read the abstract. They solve the dimer-dimer surface reaction model (or voter model) exactly in arbitrary dimension D. The density of reactive interfaces is found to exhibit a power law decay for D < 2 and a slow logarithmic decay in two dimensions.
- **Universality-class paper:** Dornic, Chaté, Chave & Hinrichsen, PRL 87, 045701 (2001). The arXiv text says voter coarsening is characterized by a slow, logarithmic decay of the density of interfaces ρ∼1/ln t (as opposed to the algebraic decay of curvature-driven growth).
- **Reviews and secondary sources:**
  - Redner's "Reality-inspired voter models: A mini-review", C. R. Physique 20, 275 (2019). I saw only its reference listing and citations in the results, not its text.
  - A readable numerical study, "Percolation and coarsening in the bidimensional voter model" (arXiv 1506.05321). It states that a characteristic length ℓ(t)≃√t can be identified, [but] the density of interfaces decays as 1/ln t.

**3. Why the fingerprint doesn't look textbook**
These are my interpretations. I did not have the run's time series.
- **Interface density of 0.343.** A random 2-type start has about 0.5 unlike-neighbour pairs, so 0.343 is only modestly coarsened. That is expected, because the 2D voter model's interface density decays only as 1/ln t.
- **Low update rate.** A per-cell rate of 0.005 means few effective updates per cell unless the run is long.
- **Small lattice.** On 64×64, coarsening saturates in finite size. Two caveats:
  - The DP-like 1/ln t regime needs a long window to be seen.
  - Consensus times scale with system size. Cox's torus consensus-time result and the Bramson–Cox–Griffeath consolidation-rate result are the relevant theory. I did not verify them in this search beyond the Cox bibliographic entries.
- **Domain count.** `g_n_domains` of 5.8 is consistent with a mid-coarsening snapshot, or with a few surviving large domains.
- **Domain structure.** The voter model has no surface tension, so its domains are ragged and fractal-like rather than the smooth blobs of curvature-driven coarsening. That is another reason the pictures differ from textbook Ising/Allen–Cahn examples.

**4. Variant caveat: the MAJ programs**
- The `C.MAJ(p=0.001)` rules are not voter dynamics. Majority rule on a Moore neighbourhood is zero-temperature, curvature-driven coarsening.
- That class is documented too. Mullick & Sen (arXiv 1707.01735) study zero temperature coarsening in the Ising model in two dimensions where the spins interact within the Moore neighbourhood. They report frozen striped states, and I read both the abstract and the conclusions.
- Barros, Krapivsky & Redner (arXiv 0905.3521) show that a 2D ferromagnet quenched to zero temperature eventually converges to either a ground state or an infinitely long-lived metastable stripe state.
- The coarsening test therefore passes for a different reason in those programs: surface tension rather than interfacial noise. The noise term p=0.001 is probably not decisive. The measured features (`g_n_types`, `g_type_entropy`) cannot tell the two mechanisms apart.
- The Moore neighbourhood is also a minor change from the nearest-neighbour literature. It changes frozen-state details, not the qualitative picture.

**5. Confidence: high.**
- The base rule is exactly the voter model, and the coarsening result is classic, with analytic and numerical sources from 1986 to 2001.
- Residual uncertainty:
  - I did not read the Cox–Griffeath full text.
  - I cannot tell from the summary whether the run is in the voter-model 1/ln t regime, the MAJ curvature-driven regime or a stripe state.
  - The CF field is assumed uncoupled.

I disagree with the first pass's mechanism. My verdict is that this behaviour is **KNOWN**, and it looks like a trivial, built-in outcome rather than a genuine emergent pattern.

**What the first pass got wrong.** It assumed there is only one node type. The feature values say otherwise:
- Type entropy is 0.689 and type modularity is 0.401. Neither makes sense with one type.
- Read `kN=2/3/4` as the number of node types. The average of 2.5 components then sits right between 2 and 4, which fits roughly one cluster per type.

So this is not random-graph relaxation. Nodes keep fixed type labels and edges are always rewired to nodes of the same type, which pulls the graph apart into separate same-type groups.

**Where it is documented.** This is the frozen-opinion limit (φ = 1) of the Holme–Newman adaptive voter model, run with opinions that never change:
- Holme and Newman describe the two ingredients: opinions spread over networks, and people with the same opinion are likely to become acquainted. Their model undergoes a continuous phase transition as the balance between those two processes changes.
- In that line of work, the rewiring-dominated regime is described as an absorbing phase in a fragmented network.
- Durrett et al., "Graph fission in an evolving voter model" (PNAS 2012), and Henry, Prałat & Zhang, "Emergence of segregation in evolving social networks" (PNAS), cover the same thing: fixed or slowly changing labels plus same-type rewiring leads to segregation and fission (cited together here).

Your rules simply delete the opinion-copying step. In this family of models that is the trivial endpoint: there is no competing process, so there is no transition to find.

**Why each feature is expected:**
- **About 2.5 components, giant component about 0.5:** roughly one component per type (2–4 types), so the largest holds about 1/kN to 1/2 of the nodes. The values are averaged over kN and p.
- **High type modularity and type entropy:** these just measure the starting labels and how sorted the graph has become. The numbers fall short of complete sorting, probably because of the p = 0.1 variants or runs not yet finished.
- **Edge turnover of about 0.49:** `ALWAYS()` keeps rewiring edges that already join same-type nodes, so edges keep reshuffling inside each type group with no structural change. That is churn built into the rule, not ongoing dynamics.
- **Degree CV of about 0.65:** the usual spread of degrees in a randomly rewired graph.

**Trivial or artifact?** Trivial. The final structure is fixed in advance by the starting type labels. It passes the fragmentation test without looking like textbook examples because there is no critical point. Every value of p only changes how quickly the graph sorts itself, not where it ends up. Seeing it across 89 programs fits that: many rule variants share the same absorbing state.

**Undocumented phenomenology:** none found.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** I'm moving this down from the first pass's KNOWN-VARIANT. The first pass treated the random firing as a twist. It isn't one: random-update versions of the cyclic automaton are the original setting that the deterministic automaton was built to imitate.

**What the rule is.** This is a cyclic cellular automaton (CCA) with 4 states, the 8-cell neighbourhood and a threshold of 1. The only change is that cells don't all update every step: each one that is able to advance does so with probability 0.3. The basic rule is the textbook one: each cell remains unchanged until some neighboring cell has a modular value exactly one unit larger than that of the cell itself, at which point it copies its neighbor's value.

**The random version is documented.**
- Bramson and Griffeath studied random-update cyclic systems first. The CCA was proposed by Bramson and Griffeath as the deterministic counterpart of the cyclic particle system, in which vertices update their colors asynchronously. Firing with probability 0.3 per step is a discrete-time stand-in for that.
- The behaviour seen here, noisy wave fronts rather than clean spirals, is described directly in Fisch, Gravner and Griffeath (1991). Their abstract says the deterministic rules show nucleation of locally periodic 'ram's horns' or spirals, while corresponding random processes give rise to a variety of 'forest fire' equilibria that display large-scale stochastic wave fronts. A fingerprint that passes the spiral test but doesn't look like a textbook spiral picture is what that random regime predicts.
- With 4 colours, the mixing regime is expected. For the random system, N ≥ 5 fixates, while 3 or 4 colours clusters, meaning that contiguous regions of all one type grow arbitrarily large.
- The other programs in the class are covered too. Changing p (0.1, 0.2, 0.5) only changes the rate. Adding COPY mixes in voter-model-style imitation noise, which roughens the fronts but doesn't change what kind of behaviour this is. None of that is new behaviour, only a different rule combination.

**Genuine pattern or artifact?** It looks like a genuine emergent pattern, but a small and noisy one. All 4 types stay present in equal proportions (entropy 1.0), there are about 7 domains, a lot of interface (0.65) and steady activity (0.42). That fits short-wavelength, noisy cyclic waves on a small 64×64 grid, where only a few rough spiral cores fit and the random firing blurs the fronts. It is not frozen and not uniform noise.

One caution: a correlation length of exactly 1.0 looks like a metric that has hit its cap or been normalised, not a measured physical length. It shouldn't be read as a new feature.

**What I didn't find:** a paper running this exact set of numbers. Per your framing, that's a missing rule combination, not missing behaviour.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** This is the Vicsek model of flocking, and the behaviour is the standard noise- and density-driven transition to polar order. Nearly all of the observed fingerprint matches what the literature describes. One part is only partly checked: the fast regime where the step length (1.0) is larger than the interaction radius (0.5).

**1. Model family.** Each agent moves at constant speed. At each step it takes the average heading of neighbours within radius r and adds angular noise. This is the Vicsek model, a metric-neighbourhood alignment rule with no cohesion and no repulsion. The "same class" variants only change r, noise and speed. The eta = 3.14159 case is the full-noise end of the range (the original paper also used η = π for its density scan).

**2. Earliest source.** Vicsek, Czirók, Ben-Jacob, Cohen and Shochet, *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 75, 1226 (1995). The abstract describes particles driven at a constant absolute velocity that assume the average direction of motion of the particles in their neighbourhood with some random perturbation η added. It reports a kinetic phase transition from no transport to finite net transport through spontaneous symmetry breaking of the rotational symmetry. It also reports a noise-driven and a density-driven transition (the arXiv version has a figure of order versus density at fixed η = π).

**3. The behaviour: high polar order together with strong density inhomogeneity.**
- Grégoire & Chaté, *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 92, 025702 (2004). Their abstract finds the transition in two space dimensions, is always discontinuous, including for the minimal model of Vicsek et al.. The apparent continuous character is due to strong finite-size effects.
- Bands and inhomogeneity are the standard picture near onset. A review essay summarises it as high density ordered bands traveling in a low density disordered background.
- Chaté, Ginelli, Grégoire & Raynaud, *Phys. Rev. E* 77, 046113 (2008), "Collective motion of self-propelled particles interacting without cohesion". I only saw this in other papers' reference lists, not as an abstract, so I'm not relying on its content.
- Reviews:
  - Ginelli, "The Physics of the Vicsek model", *Eur. Phys. J. Spec. Top.* 225, 2099 (2016). A snippet from it describes the flocking transition as a liquid-gas transition in the canonical ensemble leading to metastability, hysteresis and (micro) phase coexistence.
  - Chaté, "Dry aligning dilute active matter", *Annu. Rev. Condens. Matter Phys.* 11, 189 (2020). I only saw this one cited in a reference list.
  - Vicsek & Zafeiris, "Collective motion", *Phys. Rep.* 517, 71 (2012), also seen only as a reference-list entry.

**4. Does the fingerprint match?**
- **Polar order 0.855 with density CV 1.18 and nearest-neighbour ratio 0.82.** This fits a flock that is ordered but clumped, which is the band or cluster picture above. The nearest-neighbour ratio below 1 indicates clustering. A fluctuation-driven, inhomogeneous onset is also reported for other neighbour rules. Examples are the k-nearest-neighbour Vicsek model (present in both metric models … and in 'topological' ones) and the Voronoi version.
- **Low local alignment (0.553) next to high global order.** This is ordinary for a noisy metric rule that averages over few neighbours.
- **Why it may not look like textbook examples.** The setup is unusual in two ways:
  - **Interaction radius.** r = 0.5 at density 1 means a mean of about 0.2–0.8 neighbours per agent, much sparser than the textbook r = 1.
  - **Speed.** v = 1 with r = 0.5 means agents move more than an interaction radius per step. That is a fast, well-mixed regime.
  
  Low-speed and low-density regimes have their own literature (Rubio Puzzo et al., *PRE* 99, 052602, 2019, seen only in a reference list). I found no source for this exact high v/r regime. I read it as a parameter-range difference, not a new phenomenon, but I did not verify that. The v = 0.3 and r = 3 variants sit in more conventional ranges.
- **Angular momentum 0.098 and step 7.12.** Low angular momentum is what you'd expect in a periodic box with no vortex formation. I could not identify what the "a_step" metric measures, so I can't judge it.

**5. Confidence: medium-high.** The model identification and the order-plus-banding behaviour are well documented, and I checked the primary sources and the Grégoire–Chaté abstract. Confidence is not higher because I didn't find a paper using this exact parameter set (r = 0.5, v = 1, noise 1.0 at density 1). I also couldn't interpret the step metric. The two "shared lattice or fields" configurations mentioned at the start are not described by the rule given, so I did not assess them.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** The rule is bootstrap percolation (a k-threshold contagion) on an Erdős–Rényi-type random graph, with a random activation delay added.

**1. Model family.** Type-0 nodes flip to type 1 when at least 3 neighbours are type 1, and nothing ever flips back. That is r-neighbour bootstrap percolation with r=3 on a sparse random graph. The same dynamics appear in the social-science literature as the Watts threshold cascade model and as k-complex contagion.

The extra "p=0.1 per step" does not change the final state. A node that is eligible to flip stays eligible, because type-1 neighbours never revert, so the probability only slows the timing. It is an asynchronous or stochastic version of the same monotone process.

**2. The behaviour in the literature.** A monotone threshold process spreads from a random initial set to near-total consensus on type 1. Some nodes are left stuck at type 0 because they have too few neighbours or are locked in a cluster. This is the textbook result for this model, and I found no difference in kind.

- **Earliest source:** Chalupa, Leath and Reich, "Bootstrap percolation on a Bethe lattice", J. Phys. C 12, L31 (1979). I checked the title and year only through citing papers (introduced in 1979 in the context of magnetic disordered systems). I did not read the paper itself. Its abstract, as quoted in a search result, says for m≥3 on a Bethe lattice the infinite-cluster fraction jumps discontinuously from zero at the threshold. That is the first-order, all-or-nothing transition behind the consensus seen here.
- **Same model on random graphs:** Janson, Łuczak, Turova and Vallier, "Bootstrap percolation on the random graph G(n,p)", Ann. Appl. Probab. 22(5), 1989–2047 (2012). They study inactive vertices with at least r≥2 active neighbours becoming active. Active vertices never become inactive, so the active set only grows. A follow-up paper summarises the result: there is a sharp threshold, above which all except o(n) vertices are eventually infected.
- **Social-science version:** Watts, PNAS 2002, "A simple model of global cascades on random networks". It is a sparse random network of agents whose decisions follow a simple threshold rule. It was simulated on n=10,000 random graphs. Centola and Macy (AJS 2007) treat the k-threshold version as complex contagion, which requires social affirmation from multiple sources.
- **Review:** Adler and Lev, "Bootstrap Percolation: Visualizations and Applications", Braz. J. Phys. 33(3), 2003. It describes bootstrap percolation models and their connection with the mathematical literature. Janson's slides give a compact summary of the random-graph case. A more recent review is Morris, "Monotone cellular automata" (2017), which I saw only as a reference-list entry and did not open.

**3. Why the fingerprint looks atypical.**
- **Small graph, low degree.** With N=200 and mean degree 4, a node needs 3 active neighbours but has only about 4 links. The threshold is therefore close to the node's whole neighbourhood. Poisson degree variation, with CV about 0.5, leaves many low-degree nodes that can never reach the threshold.
- **Consensus is partial.** That explains why the consensus gain is only 0.277 and the type entropy stays at 0.474 rather than going to zero. This matches the known incomplete cascade of finite sparse graphs, and I take it to be a finite-size, low-degree effect (my inference, not tested here).
- **n_components and n_giant.** I assumed these describe the graph itself. In an ER graph with mean degree 4, the giant component holds about 98% of nodes, which fits n_giant=0.987. I did not confirm how the "components" feature is defined.
- **Oscillation is near zero (0.063).** That is what a monotone, absorbing process should give.

**4. The other rules in the class.** I only searched the main rule (threshold-3 contagion with p=0.1). The others are not all this model.
- `CNT_LE(b=0,th=3) -> SET(b=0)` is the mirror-image threshold rule, so it is the same thing.
- `NEXT_GE(th=3)` is a threshold rule too.
- `N.CYCLE`, `N.GAME` and `N.KURA` are cyclic, game-theoretic and Kuramoto-like rules. They are different families, and I did not check them. Treat the verdict as covering the threshold-contagion members only.

**5. Confidence: high** that the threshold-contagion behaviour is known. Several independent sources describe the same process, including a rigorous treatment of the same graph class. Two points stop me going further:
- I did not read the 1979 paper directly.
- I did not look for studies of the exact stochastic-delay variant. Since the delay cannot change the final state, I expect it to matter little.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** I'm downgrading the first pass's KNOWN-VARIANT. What this system does is threshold-driven cyclic coarsening that freezes in place (fixation), on a finite random graph. The ways its fingerprint differs from textbook consensus are mostly explained by the graph's structure, not by any new dynamics.

**1. The behaviour is documented.** Raising the threshold in a cyclic cellular automaton is known to switch it from endless cycling to freezing. The standard description says that the CCA has three generic forms of long-term behavior, depending on the size of the threshold relative to the range, and that at high thresholds, the CCA forms homogeneous blocks of solid colors, which are completely static — so-called fixation behavior. On the Moore neighbourhood (8 neighbours), fixation occurs with T≥4. That is a threshold of about half the neighbourhood. Here the threshold is 2 against an average of 4 links, the same ratio, so freezing into a few large single-type blocks is what you'd expect.

**2. The random-network setting is also covered.** Gravner, Lyu and Sivakoff studied the 3-colour version on arbitrary graphs and establish a phase transition on the Erdős–Rényi random graph. Their work covers the threshold-1, synchronous case, not exactly this one. Separately, in finite cyclic-dominance (rock-paper-scissors) populations, random fluctuations can push the system to the extinction of at least one of the three strategies (there are three points on the boundary corresponding to the survival of only one strategy). Szolnoki and Szabó (Phys. Rev. E 70, 037102, 2004) cover rock-paper-scissors on several network types. The combination of θ=2, probability 0.1 and asynchronous updates is just an untested parameter set. It isn't a new kind of behaviour.

**3. Why the fingerprint isn't textbook: mostly a graph artifact.** These figures are my own arithmetic, not from a source:
- In a random graph with 200 nodes and average degree 4, about 0.09 of nodes (e^-4·(1+4)) have fewer than 2 links. That's roughly 18 nodes, about 3–4 of them with no links at all. With a threshold of 2, these nodes can never change, so they keep their random starting type for good.
- Small separate pieces of the graph (n_components > 1, n_giant ≈ 0.99) can't follow the main cluster either.
- Together these leave a floor of mixed types that won't go away. That explains why consensus is only partial (gain 0.488) and why type entropy stays at 0.512.
- n_degree_cv is a property of the graph itself, not the dynamics.
- n_cyclic_changes (0.443) is the expected burst of cyclic invasions before the system freezes.
- The class also contains copy-the-majority rules that behave the same way. That suggests the shared outcome is generic "local majority-like coarsening, then fixation", not something specific to the cyclic rule.

**Is it a real emergent pattern?** Partly. The coarsening into blocks is real, known self-organisation. The "non-textbook" part of the fingerprint is trivial, a mix of finite size and frozen low-degree nodes. To check this, you could rerun on a graph where every node has at least 2 links (minimum degree 2, or a random regular graph). If consensus then becomes complete or near-complete, the artifact explanation is confirmed.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** This is the Nowak–May spatial Prisoner's Dilemma with synchronous imitate-the-best updating. T=1.9 sits inside the chaotic window.

**1. Model family.** Cells on a 64×64 torus have 8 neighbours plus self-interaction. They play a two-strategy Prisoner's Dilemma with R=1, P=0, S=0 and T=b=1.9. Every cell then copies the strategy of the highest-scoring cell in its 3×3 neighbourhood. This is the spatial evolutionary Prisoner's Dilemma, also called the Nowak–May model or the spatial game with "imitate the best neighbour".

The match is exact on each point:
- Nowak and May's setup is described as follows: players play the PD with nearest neighbouring sites and with their own site, a 3x3 territory. Each site is then taken by the player with the highest score among the previous owner and the immediate neighbours.
- The payoffs match too. Following Nowak and May, S=P=0, R=1, T=b with 1<b<2.
- The Nowak–May analysis gives a 2x2 or larger D cluster that keeps growing at its corners for b>1.8, and shrinking for b<1.8. Together with the C-cluster condition for b<2, this gives the chaotic window of roughly 1.8<b<2.

**2. Earliest source and reviews.**
- **Earliest source:** Nowak, M.A. & May, R.M., "Evolutionary games and spatial chaos", *Nature* 359, 826–829 (1992). The search confirms the citation details, and the paper was published 29 October 1992. The long-form follow-up is Nowak & May (1993), "The spatial dilemmas of evolution", *Int. J. Bifurcation Chaos* 3, 35–78. I confirmed this only from reference lists (for example). I did not read the paper itself.
- **Reviews:** Szabó & Fáth, "Evolutionary games on graphs", *Physics Reports* 446, 97–216 (2007). Its section 6.5 covers the spatial PD with synchronized update. It says in 1992 Nowak and May introduced a spatial evolutionary game to show that local interactions can maintain cooperation indefinitely. Two others are the Izquierdo et al. textbook chapter and a recent arXiv paper.
  - The textbook chapter on this model ("a model analyzed by Nowak and May (1992, 1993)") reports that the fraction of cooperators fluctuates around 0.318 for most initial conditions, using b=1.85.
  - The recent arXiv paper says Nowak and May observed that deterministic "imitate-the-best" updating generates chaotic dynamics in the spatial Prisoner's Dilemma.

**3. Does the observed fingerprint contradict the known behaviour?** I found nothing that does.
- The chemical field (D=0.1–0.2, and 0.01 in one variant) is not coupled to the game. The rule lists show only `C.GAME`, and the pure-C variant has no field at all. The field is therefore a bystander, and the same behaviour appears with and without it. It cannot change the cell dynamics. I am inferring this from the rule listing, not from a mechanism I could check.
- The metrics fit the Nowak–May regime:
  - 2 types and type entropy of 0.90 mean C and D coexist, with a C fraction a bit below 0.5. I have not matched this against the ~0.32 asymptote above, because random starts and 8-neighbour counting may differ.
  - Many small domains (about 4.3) and a short correlation length (2.5) fit a fragmented, ever-changing "kaleidoscope" of clusters.
  - The "largest domain = 0.674" figure may just reflect the connected-component definition. A near-percolating C background would give that.
- The mismatch with textbook pictures is probably a matter of initial condition. The textbook figures show a single D invading a C lattice (symmetric fractals), or an initial C fraction of about 90%. This run starts from a random 50/50 mix. Nowak and May also describe the random-start case, so the route is not new. I read only secondary descriptions of that case, not the original figures.
- One caveat on the 64×64 torus with self-interaction: the original paper used fixed boundaries and also considered tori. The sources say the conclusions are robust to this, and I did not verify that further.

**Confidence: high** that the model and behaviour are documented. The rule is the canonical Nowak–May model, and the "standard test" passing is consistent with that. I did not search for a source for the specific numerical metrics. They are generic descriptors and do not need one.

**Verdict: KNOWN-VARIANT.** The variant is minor and probably doesn't matter.

**1. Model family**
- This is a spatial evolutionary game on a lattice with two pure strategies ("C" with kC=2 types). Each cell uses the imitate-the-best-neighbour rule, also called unconditional imitation or best-takes-over.
- Each cell updates with probability p. That makes it a partially asynchronous, or "α-synchronous", version of the Nowak–May model. With p=1 it is fully synchronous. Small p approaches random sequential updating.
- I could not confirm what g=(1.5, 0.5) means, because the rule notation is not defined anywhere I could read.
  - One reading is a temptation value of 1.5 and a second payoff parameter of 0.5. If that second parameter is the "sucker" payoff, with R=1 and P=0, the game is a snowdrift or Hawk–Dove game, not a Prisoner's Dilemma.
  - The other reading is a Prisoner's Dilemma in Nowak–May form.
  - The observed result is a stable coexistence of two types. The type entropy of 0.995 is nearly 1 bit, which is consistent with either reading.

**2. Specific behaviour and sources**
- **Earliest source for the rule.** Nowak & May, "Evolutionary games and spatial chaos", Nature 359:826–829 (1992). Each site is occupied either by its original owner or by one of the neighbours, depending on who scores the highest total in that round. The rule is unconditional imitation, also known as imitate-the-best: each player takes the strategy of the neighbour with the largest payoff. C and D players coexist, with clusters of both types expanding, colliding and fragmenting.
- **Update-probability variant.** Huberman & Glance, PNAS 90:7716 (1993), re-ran the same computations in both synchronous and asynchronous fashion. They reported that defection is the dominant outcome under asynchronous updating, for at least the parameter they tested.
- **Rebuttal.** Nowak, Bonhoeffer & May, PNAS 91:4877 (1994), argued that Huberman and Glance had analyzed this contrast only for a single value of the cheating-advantage parameter, so the conclusion they draw is misleading. They reported that for other b values, patterns settle into a mostly static C/D coexistence.
- **Intermediate asynchrony (the p parameter).** Grilo & Correia, J. Theor. Biol. 269:109 (2011), studied exactly this setup. Only a fraction of the agents update their behaviour each time. They found cooperation changes smoothly and monotonically from synchronous to sequential dynamics. Their synchrony rate α is the probability that each agent is chosen at each iteration. I could only read the abstract of this paper, not the full text.
- **Review.** Roca, Cuesta & Sánchez, "Evolutionary game theory: Temporal and spatial effects beyond replicator dynamics" (Phys. Life Rev. 2009), has a section on synchronous versus asynchronous update. It calls the Huberman and Glance result one of the best-known examples of why update synchronicity matters. Szabó & Fáth, "Evolutionary games on graphs" (Phys. Rep. 2007), covers the synchronised-update spatial Prisoner's Dilemma at the start of its section 6.5.
- **If the game is snowdrift or Hawk–Dove.** Killingback & Doebeli, Proc. R. Soc. B 263:1135 (1996), ran the same best-takes-over lattice dynamics for Hawk–Dove. A statistical-physics review describes both models as essentially two-dimensional cellular automata displaying a variety of spatio-temporal patterns and even chaos. Hauert & Doebeli, Nature 428:643 (2004), is the standard snowdrift reference. I only confirmed these two through citation lists and abstracts.

**3. What differs, and whether it matters**
- The rule system sweeps p over 0.003 to 0.3. This is the intermediate-asynchrony regime of Grilo & Correia, plus the nearly sequential limit. At p=0.003 there is still some synchrony, but nearly sequential updating is a good description.
- I did not find a source that reports the particular "spatial chaos" fingerprint here, which is about six domains, zero or one reversals and a correlation length of 1.
  - This is probably not new. My reading is that low p turns Nowak–May's chaotic, constantly flipping dynamics into slow, near-static coexistence of domains. That matches Nowak–Bonhoeffer–May's description of patterns settling to a mostly static state, and Grilo & Correia's smooth change with synchrony.
  - The "standard test" here probably only checks for persistent coexistence of the two types. That is not the same as true Nowak–May chaos, and the mismatch with textbook examples most likely comes from that difference.
- Remaining uncertainty: I could not read the notation for g, and I could not verify the exact payoff regime. If g defines a snowdrift-type game, the Killingback–Doebeli line is the closer precedent, not Nowak–May. That would not change the verdict.

**4. Confidence: medium.** The model family, the rule and the p-update variant are clearly documented. Confidence is not high for three reasons. I did not read the full texts of the key papers. The meaning of g is ambiguous. I did not find a source describing this exact observable fingerprint.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** I'm treating it as KNOWN rather than a variant because the differences from the textbook model look like implementation details. They are not a different mechanism.

**1. Model family**
- This is the adaptive (co-evolving) voter model with rewire-to-same.
- Each node copies a random neighbour's type. A node that has a discordant link cuts it and reconnects to a random node of its own type.
- This version has 3 states instead of 2.
- The "SAME CLASS" variants add copy probabilities below 1 and a FLIP rule with a spontaneous-change probability. Those are the noisy adaptive voter model.
- The CYCLE variants have a cyclic-dominance, rock-paper-scissors-like update and are discussed separately in point 3.

**2. The behaviour and its sources**
- **Earliest clear source:** Holme & Newman (2006) introduced the model with G opinions. They found a continuous phase transition as the balance parameter is varied, from a regime where opinions are arbitrarily diverse to one where most individuals hold the same opinion. I read this through the arXiv and Semantic Scholar pages.
- **Closest source to the three-state behaviour I observed:** Böhme & Gross, "Fragmentation transitions in multistate voter models", Phys. Rev. E 85, 066117. It studies models with an arbitrary number of opinions and gives detailed analytical results for a three-opinion model, confirmed by agent-based simulations.
- **Review-level sources:**
  - Böhme & Gross (arXiv 1012.1213) give an analytical approach for calculating the transition point in general adaptive network models.
  - The Durrett et al. PNAS 2012 paper on graph fission confirms that the rewire-to-same model has a phase transition similar to Holme and Newman's.
  - I did not find a dedicated review article.
- **Fragmentation outcome:** The standard result is a fragmented state in which the network splits into components that are each internally in consensus. For the directed model, the network breaks into at least two components, which are internally in consensus.
- **Rewiring rates:** Fragmentation occurs above a critical rewiring rate (see the numerical results in the zealotry paper, arXiv 1612.06644).

**3. Why the fingerprint looks non-textbook**
- **Update scheme:**
  - In the usual model, one random edge or node is updated per step, so rewiring stays below a critical rate.
  - Here every node copies and rewires at every step (p=1), which is a synchronous, very fast rewiring regime.
  - Rewiring at this strength should sit deep in the fragmented phase. I did not find a source that studies this synchronous variant explicitly, but I don't expect it to change the mechanism.
- **High edge turnover (0.891) alongside fragmentation:**
  - In the noise-free model, fragmentation is absorbing. Once no discordant links remain, rewiring stops.
  - Turnover therefore comes from the transient, or from noise. The FLIP and CYCLE members of the class keep injecting discordant links.
  - Noisy adaptive voter models are discussed in the zealotry paper's noise section, and in the noisy-AVM moment-closure paper (arXiv 1812.05464). That paper adds a small random mutation term, which makes the system ergodic.
  - This is likely the main reason the fingerprint differs from the textbook one. It is a known ingredient, but I found no paper that reports this exact fingerprint: fragmented communities with persistent, high link turnover.
- **Three-type entropy of 1.0:** Three types surviving in separate clusters matches the multistate fragmented phase.
- **CYCLE variants:** These match Demirel et al., "Cyclic dominance in adaptive networks". In each step a link is selected and an RPS game is played, and the loser either adopts the winner's opinion or rewires the link. A related paper (Epj B 2017) reports a frozen phase with three separate clusters using only R, P, and S, with adaptive actions terminated.

**4. Confidence: medium-high.**
- The model family, the fragmentation transition and the multistate version are clearly documented in sources I could read.
- The two weak points are the synchronous, every-node-every-step update and the persistent turnover under noise. I found no paper that studies either on its own.
- I did not run a dedicated search for the synchronous-update variant.
- The remaining worry is that the "n_components=1.461" statistic is on an unknown scale, so I can't check it against published numbers.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** The system is a standard adaptive (coevolving) voter model, with a few implementation differences that probably don't change the outcome.

**1. Model family.** This is the adaptive or coevolving voter model on a random graph. Nodes copy a random neighbour's state (voter dynamics). Nodes that sit on a discordant link cut it and rewire to a random same-state node ("rewire-to-same"). The model has 3 states, an Erdős–Rényi network with mean degree about 4, and a low rewiring probability (0.1) compared with copying (1.0).

**2. Earliest clear sources for this behaviour.**
- **Holme & Newman (2006), Phys. Rev. E 74, 056108.**
  - This is the earliest clear match. Their model has G opinions and rewiring to same-opinion nodes.
  - The model reaches a consensus state in finite time on a finite network.
  - The structure of the consensus state shows clear signatures of a continuous phase transition as the balance between opinion change and rewiring is varied.
  - Related work (Durrett et al.) describes the dynamics ending when no edges join different opinions. In that setting the end state is either a single connected consensus or several clusters, each in internal consensus (Kozma & Barrat, in the bounded-confidence version).
- **Vazquez, Eguíluz & San Miguel (2008), PRL 100, 108702.**
  - A discordant link is rewired with probability p; otherwise a node takes its neighbour's state.
  - There is an absorbing transition from an active to a frozen phase at p_c = (μ−2)/(μ−1).
  - The active and frozen phases correspond to a connected and a fragmented network.
  - At mean degree 4, p_c = 2/3 in their parametrisation. Rewiring at 0.1 against copying at 1.0 is well below that, so the network stays connected and ends in consensus.
- **Review.** Durrett et al. (2012), PNAS "Graph fission in an evolving voter model", covers this exact rewire-to-same variant. It reports a phase transition similar to Holme and Newman's. The Gross & Sayama-type review "Adaptive Dynamical Networks" (arXiv 2304.05652) also covers it. At low rewiring rates there is an extended dynamical phase followed by eventual consensus. Past a critical rewiring rate that dynamical phase vanishes.
- **Multi-state version.** "Fragmentation transitions in multi-state voter models" is relevant to the 3-state case. It gives detailed analytical results for a three-opinion model.
- **Consensus-time scaling.** Rogers & Gross (2013), "Consensus time and conformity in the adaptive voter model" (arXiv 1304.4742), covers the update-rule variants. It lists edge, node-direct and node-reverse updates, plus rewire-to-same and rewire-to-random.

**3. How the observed features map onto the literature.**
- **Consensus gain with a giant component of about 0.99.** This is the low-rewiring, active route to consensus. The network stays connected and a single opinion wins, rather than the network fragmenting. This matches the active/connected phase.
- **High edge turnover.** This is expected, because rewiring continues while discordant links exist.
- **n_components = 1.304.** This presumably reflects a few isolated nodes or small clusters alongside the giant component. I could not verify how that metric is defined. It looks like transient or finite-size fragmentation, which is also standard.
- **Oscillation (0.377) and degree CV (0.485).** Rewire-to-same attachment produces a broad degree distribution, and the random-walk-like fluctuations in state counts before absorption account for the oscillation. I did not find a paper that reports these two metrics specifically. They look like ordinary by-products of the same dynamics rather than a separate phenomenon.

**4. Differences from the textbook models.** I judge that none of them likely matters.
- **Update scheme.** Copying and rewiring both happen in each step, and every node copies (p=1.0). The textbook models choose one event per update, either copy or rewire. This is a synchronous-style, discrete-time version. It mainly changes the effective time-scale ratio between rewiring and copying. The literature supports this: in a different opinion model, asynchronous updating changed only time scales and not the qualitative results. Rewire-first and copy-first orders (the other class members) should also be equivalent.
- **Three states.** Holme–Newman already used G opinions.
- **The GAME variant with g=(1.5, −0.5).** This replaces copying with a game-based update rule. I did not search for this variant specifically. It is a different imitation rule (an evolutionary game on an adaptive network), but it is plausibly in the same consensus/fragmentation class. It is the part least covered by my search.

**5. Confidence: medium-high.** The core system, its connected-consensus outcome, and the control parameters are all well documented. I did not find a source for the exact synchronous "every node copies each step" implementation, or for the specific metric fingerprint. The remaining uncertainty is about those details, not about the phenomenon.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** The behaviour is consensus in a multi-state voter model on a sparse random graph, plus a separate diffusive phase-synchronisation (Kuramoto-type) process on the same graph. **1. Model family**
- The type-copying rule is the **multi-state voter model** on an Erdős–Rényi graph with mean degree 4. Each node adopts a random neighbour's type, here with probability 0.1 per step. Starnini et al. describe the voter model as a process where a random node is selected and copies the state of one of its neighbors, and they extend it to any number of states.
- The phase rule is a **Kuramoto-type phase-oscillator network**. Each node is pulled toward its neighbours' phases, and the description gives no natural-frequency term. I read that as pure diffusive coupling, which is a discrete-time consensus or Laplacian-averaging process. This is my reading of the rule, not something the search confirmed.
- As described, neither layer feeds back on the other. The system is two independent processes sharing one graph.
- The `N.REWIRE(p=0.003)` member of the class puts it near **adaptive (coevolving) voter models**. The Holme–Newman model has a continuous phase transition between diverse opinions and consensus. Rewiring can also fragment the graph, which would explain the high `n_components`.

**2. Earliest clear sources and a review**
- **Voter model, original.** Clifford & Sudbury (1973) and Holley & Liggett (1975). I only saw these in a reference list (Biometrika 60(3):581-588 and Ann. Probab. 3(4):643–663), not as the papers themselves. The citations are checked, but I did not read the papers.
- **Multi-state voter model.** Starnini, Baronchelli & Pastor-Satorras, J. Stat. Mech. P10027 (2012). They treat the number of states as a parameter that can assume any value, from 2 to ∞.
- **Voter-model review.** Redner, "Reality Inspired Voter Models: A Mini-Review", Comptes rendus – Physique 20, 275 (2019) (arXiv:1811.11888).
- **Voter model on random graphs.** For the standard voter model on complete graphs and Erdős–Rényi networks, the consensus time scales linearly with system size. At N=200 that makes consensus reachable in a finite run, which fits the high `n_consensus_gain`.
- **Adaptive voter model.** Holme & Newman, Phys. Rev. E 74, 056108 (2006), found by search (arXiv:physics/0603023). Durrett et al., PNAS 2012, covers rewire-to-same and rewire-to-random variants.
- **Kuramoto on networks, review.** Arenas et al. (the Physics Reports review, also available as "The Kuramoto model: a simple paradigm for synchronization phenomena", Acebrón et al.). The latter says coupling matrices K_ij have been considered such as nearest-neighbor coupling, hierarchical coupling, random long-range coupling. A second review is Dörfler & Bullo's "Synchronization in Complex Networks of Phase Oscillators".
- **Network consensus.** In the Kuramoto network literature, synchronisation is equivalent to the formation of consensus in society when phases are read as beliefs.
- **Voter model and Kuramoto side by side.** The "Dynamical Systems on Networks: A Tutorial" treats them as separate canonical node dynamics, noting that the oscillator model provides an interesting contrast to the contagion and voter models.

**3. Searches for the specific combination**
- I searched for a voter model coupled to Kuramoto oscillators, and for discrete opinion state combined with oscillator phase on a coevolving network. Only unrelated hits came back: Kuramoto used as an opinion model, a "voting Kuramoto" decision model, discrete-phase Kuramoto, and Kuramoto with contrarians.
- I found no paper on an uncoupled voter layer plus Kuramoto layer on one random graph. Such a system is trivially the product of two known processes. It is probably not worth a paper, which is why it isn't described.

- Two independent ordering processes are being scored together.

- The `n_oscillation` and `n_type_entropy` values most likely reflect finite-size, finite-time transients. I could not check these two against any source.
- In the rewiring variant, fragmentation is the known adaptive-network effect.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** This is not documented as a new form of spatial game chaos, and the "chaos" label is probably an artifact of the noise. The first pass was right about the noise but too generous in calling it a variant. Nothing in what was observed needs a new mechanism.

**1. The game is a snowdrift game, not a Prisoner's Dilemma.** With T=1.5 > R=1 > S=0.5 > P=0, the payoffs are in the snowdrift (hawk–dove) order. Hauert & Doebeli showed that in unstructured snowdrift games, intermediate levels of cooperation persist. Unexpectedly, spatial structure reduces the proportion of cooperators for a wide range of parameters. They also describe the spatial patterns: while in the spatial prisoner's dilemma cooperators can survive by forming large, compact clusters, in the spatial snowdrift game cooperators form only small filament-like clusters. That is, it is advantageous to adopt strategies that are opposite to neighboring strategies. Small, broken-up clusters fit the short correlation length (2) and the several small domains (about 5). Also, the well-mixed snowdrift equilibrium is (S−P)/[(S−P)+(T−R)] = 0.5/1.0 = **0.5 cooperators**. That would give a type entropy close to 1, which matches the observed 0.989. My reading is that the system behaves like a randomly mixed snowdrift population sitting at its textbook coexistence point.

**2. The mixing steps are a documented ingredient.** Copying a random neighbour every step (a voter-model step) or swapping with a neighbour at p=1.0 is very strong random mixing. Random movement in lattice games has been studied: one line of work used movement that was Brownian random walk like, i.e. diffusive, not relying on any type of explicit, genotypic or phenotypic assortment, and also being strategy-independent. Comparisons across games found that random migration plays the cooperation inhibiting role in spatial structures in the SDG, while playing the cooperation enhancing role in PDG and SHG. Vainstein & Arenzon present an extensive, systematic study of the Prisoner's Dilemma and Snowdrift games on a square lattice under a synchronous, noiseless imitation dynamics, including random mobility. Their setup is the closest published match to the SWAP and GAME versions in this class.

**3. Why the chaos test result is probably an artifact.** Nowak–May chaos is defined as a purely deterministic, spatial version of the Prisoners' Dilemma that produces chaotically changing spatial patterns. Here a random step (copy or swap at p=1.0) runs every step, so two copies of the run will drift apart in Hamming distance whatever the game does. Even work that measures chaos this way notes that in the case of the game exhibiting a degree of stochasticity, the distance increases more rapidly. That is why the test can't tell real chaos from plain noise here. The activity of 0.46 and the single reversal look like noise churning around a mixed equilibrium, not the shifting patterns Nowak and May described.

**Caveats:**
- **The g=(1.3, 0.0) member doesn't fit the snowdrift explanation.** With S=P it is the weak Prisoner's Dilemma, whose mixed-population outcome is all defectors. It still lands in the same fingerprint class, probably because the random step keeps both types around. That supports the idea that the noise sets the fingerprint, not the game. I can't confirm from here that it actually sits at the same roughly 50/50 split.
- **The domain count is ambiguous.** A value of about 5 could just as well describe random speckle; it isn't evidence of structure.
