**Verdict: KNOWN.** This is ordinary two-type majority-rule domain coarsening with mixing (stirring), ending in the usual finite-lattice outcomes: either one type takes over or a few large domains/stripes remain. I couldn't find any feature of the behaviour that is new. The fact that this exact rule combination isn't in the literature doesn't count as a discovery.

**What each ingredient maps to**
- **Majority flips plus neighbour swaps.** This is the Glauber-plus-Kawasaki (spin-flip plus stirring) setup. Studies of it look at interacting spin (particle) systems on a lattice under the combined influence of spin flip (Glauber) and simple exchange (Kawasaki) dynamics. When swaps are fast, the macroscopic density... evolves according to an autonomous nonlinear diffusion-reaction equation. Majority rule with moving agents has also been studied directly: a diffusive majority-vote model in which spins are allowed to jump to a random neighbor node... and in the second stage, the spins in the same node can change its values according to the majority-vote update rule. It shows a consensus phase.
- **Why the swaps matter.** Updated all at once, majority rule on its own gets stuck. On a finite grid, every trajectory eventually reaches a fixed point or a cycle of period two. The swaps break these frozen or flip-flopping states, so coarsening can continue. That is the documented role of noise or stirring, not a new mechanism.
- **Where it ends up.** In 2D at zero noise, the system reaches either a frozen stripe state with probability approximately 1/3 or the ground state with probability approximately 2/3. With periodic edges the predicted stripe probability is about 0.3390….

**Reading the fingerprint**
- **g_corrlen = 14:** about L/4.5 on a 64×64 grid, so domain size is nearing the system size. This is late-stage coarsening that is running into the lattice size.
- **Negative activity trend, activity_cv = 0.7:** flips and visible swaps only happen at domain boundaries. Activity therefore tracks total boundary length, which shrinks as domains grow, with bursts when domains merge or disappear.
- **g_n_types = 1.667, g_n_domains = 1.29:** this looks like a mix of runs where one type wins and runs where both survive as one or two large domains. That is the consensus-or-stripes split described above. Read it with care, though. If 1.667 averages 3 seeds, it means 2 of 3 runs kept both types, which is more stripe-like endings than the ~1/3 benchmark. The swaps may also keep stripe boundaries wandering rather than frozen. Either way, this is a known finite-size effect with too few runs to be a new phenomenon.
- **g_reversals = 1.0:** probably one change in direction (an early transient, then decay). This is consistent with normal coarsening and not a sign of anything else.
- **Same class across 6 programs:** the related programs (majority at p=0.1, sandpile toppling plus majority, an added diffusing field) all give the same result. That points to generic ordering behaviour, not a quirk of one rule set.

**Why it doesn't look textbook:** it uses 8 neighbours, updates every cell at once, and has strong stirring. It is also measured on a small grid where domains approach system size, so there is no clean power-law growth, and the end states are a mix of outcomes. These are effects of grid size and how the run was measured, not a new route to ordering. The coarsening itself is real, but nothing about this form of it is new.

**What the game is.** With T=1.5 > R=1 > S=0.5 > P=0, this is a snowdrift (hawk-dove) game, not a prisoner's dilemma. The two games differ only in whether P or S is ranked higher. In a snowdrift game on a lattice, it pays to adopt the opposite of your neighbours' strategy, so spatial structure ends up inhibiting cooperation, as Hauert & Doebeli showed (Nature 428, 643–646, 2004). The usual result is that both types coexist: one forms a large connected region and the other survives as small scattered patches. That matches what was seen. A largest domain of 0.835 and a type entropy of 0.654 bits mean roughly 84/16 coexistence, around 4–5 domains, and a short correlation length of about 2.

**Random movement in spatial games is well studied.** Sicardi, Fort, Vainstein & Arenzon (2009) studied an unconditional move rule in the spatial Prisoner's Dilemma, Snowdrift and Stag Hunt games. They found that random dilution and mobility may suppress the inhibiting factors of the spatial structure in the Snowdrift game.

**The swap mechanism is explicitly anticipated, not overlooked.** In the same research line, the authors note that random movement may be even independent of the occupation ρ of the lattice if implemented through, for example, the swapping of two neighboring strategies. They chose vacancy-based moves for their own reasons. On a fully occupied lattice, swapping neighbours is just a standard way to add random mixing; it doesn't create new behaviour.

**The swap isn't even needed for this behaviour.** The same class includes swap rates from 0.005 to 0.1 and a variant with copying (`C.COPY(p=0.2)`) and no swap at all. So the behaviour comes from best-neighbour imitation in the snowdrift game, and the mixing only nudges it.

**Is the pattern real or an artifact?** It's a genuine emergent pattern, the well-known one, but the summary numbers say little.
- A short correlation length (about 2) plus one dominant domain is what you'd expect when the majority type simply forms one connected region. This is a fixed level of coexistence, not ongoing growth of domains.
- So the "domain coarsening" label is probably a misreading of the metrics. The "spatial game chaos" label fits only loosely.
- A single reversal (`g_reversals=1`) is consistent with a short transient.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** This is ordinary majority-vote coarsening that ends up frozen, with the Schelling move rule doing very little. It isn't a new kind of segregation. The first pass called it KNOWN-VARIANT because the published Schelling–voter hybrids are set up differently. But the instructions say a different rule setup doesn't count as a discovery. The behaviour itself is documented.

**Why the fingerprint doesn't look like textbook Schelling.** Rule (1) is a majority vote applied to every cell at once, every step, with probability 1. On a Moore (8-neighbour) lattice this rule settles down by itself: Moore-neighbourhood majority-vote CAs are Class 1, converging to a stable pattern, and converge to unanimity when one type starts with a large enough majority. Majority rule is a well-known way to model this: for dimensions above 1, majority rule is implemented as a zero-temperature spin-flip kinetic Ising model. For random-sequential majority rule, the model with an odd neighbourhood size is conjectured to cluster in any dimension. Moore (1997) studies the synchronous majority-vote CA directly and ties it to zero-temperature single spin-flip Ising dynamics.

How each observed feature follows:
- **Long correlation length, few domains, large largest domain:** majority rule grows domains, which then freeze or reach consensus.
- **Falling activity:** the system is freezing.
- **Reversals:** most likely the period-2 flip-flopping that synchronous majority rules produce at ties and interfaces (this is my inference, I didn't confirm it).
- **Fewer surviving types (g_n_types well below 3):** a key detail is that "empty" (type 0) votes in the majority rule like any other type. So the number of vacancies isn't fixed. Empty cells can form their own domains, grow, or disappear, and agent types can be voted out entirely. That's majority-vote type loss, not Schelling's conserved segregation.
- **The Schelling rule hardly matters:** once majority voting has made neighbourhoods uniform, almost no agent falls below the 0.3 tolerance threshold, so few ever move. That would explain why changing the threshold (0.6, 0.7) or the majority probability (0.1) lands in the same class.

**Is it already in the literature?** Yes. Schelling with vacancies is mathematically equivalent to the zero-temperature spin-exchange kinetic Ising model with vacancies, and its coarsening laws are measured; for example, interface density decays as a power law with exponent ≈0.5 at low vacancy density. Hybrids that mix moving and type-changing exist: in the Schelling–Voter model an unhappy agent can change her place or her state to be happy. This system is just the limiting case where type-changing (by majority) applies to everyone and wins out.

**Genuine or trivial?** The domains really do form on their own, but the result is close to trivial. One rule (majority vote) controls everything and the system heads for a frozen or near-consensus state. Calling it "segregation with vacancies" is partly a labelling artifact, because vacancies aren't conserved here.

**Caveat:** I didn't find a paper on exactly a synchronous 3-state Moore majority CA with a Schelling move step and vacancies that can be voted in or out. Under the stated criterion, that missing rule combination doesn't make the behaviour new.

**How each observed feature maps onto existing work:**

1. **Segregation and coarsening with vacancies.** The noisy Schelling model with vacancies has a mapped phase diagram with three phases: frozen, segregated and mixed. In the segregated phase, coarsening is measured as a power-law decay with an exponent α ≃ 0.5 in the interface density.
2. **Swap and copy as noise on top of Schelling moves.** This exact pairing has been studied. There are rigorous hydrodynamic-limit results for the Schelling model with spontaneous Glauber and Kawasaki dynamics, which predict a mixed, a segregated and a metastable segregation phase. Your SWAP rule plays the Kawasaki role (neighbours exchange places) and COPY plays the Glauber role (a cell's type gets replaced). A swap rate of 1 just means strong noise. That doesn't make it a new mechanism.
3. **Finite domains instead of full separation** (correlation length about 11 and about 6 domains on a 64×64 grid). Stauffer's Schelling–Ising work with tolerance and noise as temperatures reports exactly this regime: for intermediate T, we get small clusters but no large domains, and for low T the domains grow to infinite sizes. Continual swapping stops coarsening at a finite size where ordering and noise balance. That's probably why the run passes the coarsening test but doesn't look like the textbook picture.
4. **Three types.** Schelling models with Q groups are long-standing. For example, there is a Potts-like model of Q ethnic groups covering ghetto formation and its prevention by an increasing social temperature. The link to the Potts model for more than two profiles is standard.
5. **Small lattice.** Schelling-type aggregation on small lattices has its own warnings in the literature. Singh et al. argue that the global aggregation that Schelling observed is a small lattice phenomenon. A count of about 6 domains on a 64×64 grid could well depend on the lattice size.

- **Type entropy of 1.0 and 3 types:** these most likely just reflect the random equal start. Swapping conserves type counts. This assumes the entropy is normalised to its maximum.
- **Reversals of about 0.95 and the activity variability:** these are most likely the constant back-and-forth swapping at domain edges from the forced p=1 swap, not a coherent new dynamic.

**What remains unchecked:** I didn't find a paper running three equal types with an unconditional full-rate swap on 8 neighbours. That gap is in the parameters, not the behaviour. The only open questions are numbers: how the steady-state domain size depends on noise strength, threshold and lattice size. Those are standard measurements, not new phenomena.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** This is the standard two-group Schelling model with vacancies, plus random noise that limits how far segregation goes. The first pass called it KNOWN-VARIANT, and I think that's wrong for three reasons.

**1. The first pass got the type count wrong.** The rule says "3 types" but type 0 is empty. So this is the usual setup: two kinds of agents plus vacancies. The literature uses exactly this encoding: each site takes one of three values: ±1 for the two kinds of agents and 0 for vacancies, and agents can only move if the vacancy density is above zero. Dropping "3 types instead of 2" removes half of the first pass's case for a variant.

**2. The swap step is just noise, and Schelling with noise is well studied.** Swapping neighbours at random with probability 0.1, regardless of how satisfied they are, works like exchange dynamics at infinite temperature. In other words, it's random mixing.
- Stauffer & Solomon noted the link between the Schelling model and the Ising model for ferromagnetism, and introduced thermal fluctuations in the microscopic dynamics.
- A later study notes that letting satisfied agents move too produces a noise effect that acts like temperature in statistical physics.
- Ódor's two-temperature version found that above T₂ = 0.135, the noise breaks up the segregated, ordered domains. In a five-group version, with strong noise, segregation is greatly reduced, though gradually rather than in a sudden jump. That five-group work also covers multi-type Schelling, so even a true three-agent-type reading wouldn't be new.
- That Hazan & Randon-Furling leave out swap moves only means one paper didn't use this mechanism. It doesn't make the behaviour undocumented.

**3. The "not textbook" fingerprint is what noise-limited segregation should look like.** The measurements show short correlation length (1.67 cells), moderate spatial clustering (Moran 0.37), about 6 domains on a 64×64 grid, and frequent reversals (0.955). Together that means small domains that keep forming and dissolving: segregation held back by noise rather than coarsening fully. That matches the documented reduction or loss of segregation under noise. Many small frozen clusters are also documented without noise: restricted movement tends to freeze into small clusters ("solid-like"), while unrestricted movement lets clusters keep growing ("liquid-like"). Dall'Asta et al. report phase transitions typical of kinetically constrained models, unusual coarsening, and percolation-related effects. The high reversal score most likely comes directly from the random swaps flipping cells back and forth, so it isn't an independent feature.

**The same-class list is a warning sign about the measurements.** The 243-program class includes non-Schelling rules with 4 types (kC=4) that move cells when 3 or more neighbours are of the next type. This summary groups very different rules under one profile, which suggests the profile captures generic "weak clustering plus vacancies" rather than a specific new route to segregation.

**Genuine or artifact?** It's a real emergent pattern, but a weak one: clustering is clearly above random yet well short of full segregation. Some features are by-products of the setup. The high reversal score is almost certainly swap flicker, and the 64×64 grid limits how big domains can get. Nothing here is unexplained.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** I'm changing the first pass's KNOWN-VARIANT to KNOWN. The behaviour is mostly multi-state voter-model coarsening with some noise added. The "Schelling segregation" part is largely a labelling artifact, not a separate route to segregation.

**Why the first pass's framing doesn't hold**
- The documented Schelling–Voter hybrid works differently. There, an unhappy agent is selected at random, and she chooses to play one of two different games: either she migrates to another place where she will be happy (with probability p), or she changes her own type (with probability 1−p). In this system, every cell copies a random neighbour every step, whether or not it is unhappy.
- That makes rule (2), applied to all cells including empty ones, a synchronous voter model with three states, where "empty" is one of the states. This is my reading of the rule text, not something I measured. If it's right, vacancies are not conserved, so the vacancy mechanism behind Schelling coarsening doesn't apply as such.
- The copying rule is strong enough to swamp the move rule. That explains why 33 rule programs with thresholds from 0.2 to 0.4, either rule order and 3–4 types all give the same fingerprint. The threshold and the order barely matter.

**Why the observed fingerprint matches voter coarsening**
- The 2D voter model is a known marginal case. It coarsens through interfacial noise, not curvature. It is characterized by a slow, logarithmic decay of the density of interfaces ρ∼1/ln t (as opposed to the algebraic decay ρ∼1/L(t)∼t^(-1/z) of curvature-driven growth). It also produces patterns with clusters of all sizes between 1 and √t.
- That fits what was seen: about 6 domains, a short correlation length (about 2.3), all 3 types still present at high entropy, and frequent reversals (flickering at interfaces). On a 64×64 grid, voter coarsening hasn't finished by the end of a finite run. The Schelling moves just add noise on top.
- This also explains why it "passes the coarsening test but doesn't look like a textbook case." Schelling-type coarsening shows algebraic growth. For example, one study finds the interface density decays as a power law with an exponent α≃0.5 for the limit of small vacancy density. Voter coarsening is logarithmic and tensionless, so it looks different.
- Related variants that I did not check against this run:
  - Adding intermediate states can restore an effective surface tension.
  - Even a small number of Ising-type agents can switch the dynamics to curvature-driven growth. Even a very small (∼1%) fraction of Ising agents changes the tensionless dynamics into the curvature-driven Ising-like dynamics.
  - Schelling moves acting as noise sit within this known family of perturbed voter models.

**Genuine pattern or artifact?** The coarsening itself is real but generic: plain voter-model ordering that was still incomplete when the run stopped. Calling it "segregation with vacancies" is an artifact of how the rules are described. Updating every cell at once may increase the reversal count. I'm not aware of any feature here that a multi-state synchronous voter model with added noise wouldn't reproduce.

**What would change my verdict:** If interface density over time decays algebraically rather than as 1/ln t, or if the vacancy fraction stays constant (meaning empty cells aren't actually copied), I'd move to KNOWN-VARIANT. It would then be Schelling-driven coarsening with voter noise, closer to the hybrid model above. A t-vs-ρ log-plot would settle it.

**Verdict: KNOWN-VARIANT.** The behaviour is the fragmentation transition of the adaptive (coevolving) voter model. The variant here uses a majority-rule node update, synchronous in effect, with 3 states and rewire-to-same.

**1. Model family.** This is an adaptive-network opinion model. Node states update from their neighbours, and links between discordant nodes are rewired. Rewiring goes to a node of the same state, which is the "rewire-to-same" variant. Here the node update is a local majority rule, not voter-model copying of one random neighbour. There are 3 states, a random sparse graph (mean degree about 4), and N=200.

**2. Specific behaviour: network fragmentation.**
- **Earliest clear sources.**
  - Holme & Newman (2006), "Nonequilibrium phase transition in the coevolution of networks and opinions", Phys Rev E 74, 056108. The abstract describes a continuous phase transition as this parameter is varied, from a regime in which opinions are arbitrarily diverse to one in which most individuals hold the same opinion. This is rewire-to-same with many opinion states. I read the abstract only, not the full text.
  - Vazquez, Eguíluz & San Miguel (2008), PRL 100, 108702. In their model, a link between opposite-state nodes is rewired with probability p, while with probability 1-p one of the nodes takes its neighbor's state. They report that the active and frozen phases correspond to a connected and a fragmented network respectively.
- **Multi-state version.** Vazquez, González-Avella, Eguíluz & San Miguel (2007), PRE 76, 046120. They study the coevolution of network structure and node states in a model of multiple state interacting agents. They find a frozen configuration, composed by disconnected network components whose agents share the same state.
- **Rewire-to-same.** Durrett et al. (2012), PNAS, "Graph fission in an evolving voter model". Their model has an edge broken and one endpoint reconnecting to an individual chosen at random from those with the same opinion. They note that this rewire-to-same model has a phase transition similar to that of Holme and Newman.
- **Majority rule with rewiring.** Carro, Vazquez, Toral & San Miguel (2014), PRE 89, 062802. This is the closest majority-rule source. It uses the majority rule or zero-temperature Glauber dynamics on link states, plus rewiring. It finds that any amount of rewiring is able to drive the network to complete order. The final state is either one component or a network fragmented in two. It also reports a domain of bistability between fragmented and non-fragmented final states at low rewiring rates and finite size.
- **Reviews.**
  - Starnini, "Opinion dynamics: Statistical physics and beyond" (arXiv 2507.11521) mentions coevolving models leading, e.g., to fragmentation–consensus transitions as a function of the rewiring rate.
  - Moment-closure and analytic work on adaptive voter models (arXiv 1211.0449, 1012.1213) also covers the transition.
  - I did not find a single dedicated review of majority-rule adaptive networks.

**3. What differs, and whether it matters.**
- **Majority rule on nodes, with rewire-to-same and 3 states.** I did not find a paper with exactly this combination. The mechanism should carry over, because rewiring removes discordant links and node updates remove disagreement. The fixed point is the same in both: no discordant links, so the network splits into same-state components. Majority rule differs in two ways. It produces local frozen domains (disordered topological traps in Carro et al., which come from majority rule alone), and it has no voter-style noise-driven drift to consensus. So fragmentation is likely easier to reach, and the bistability with one-component outcomes may shift.
- **Probability 1.0 majority update every step, with rewiring at p=0.1 or 0.03 and the update ordering swapped.** Synchronous or every-step majority updating is not what the cited models use. They update one node or link at a time. This is likely to matter for details such as trap formation and oscillation. I would not expect it to change the fact that fragmentation occurs.
- **The unusual fingerprint.** The strong signals are `n_components` of 1.44 and `n_giant` of 0.69. The giant component is large, but there are several others. Type entropy is high (0.65), so more than one type survives. Modularity by type (0.36) and degree CV (0.46) are also elevated. This is consistent with fragmentation into multiple same-type components of unequal size, which is the multi-state fragmented absorbing phase. It also fits a partly fragmented, majority-frozen state. Multi-state models were reported to give several components (Vazquez et al. 2007). I did not find numbers for degree CV or edge turnover in the literature. Rewire-to-same is expected to make degrees heterogeneous, since nodes of a surviving type receive extra links. I did not check this against a source.
- **Short runs.** At 83 programs with low rewiring (p=0.03), the system may not have finished fragmenting. That would explain why the fingerprint differs from textbook examples. It is an inference, not something I verified.

**4. Confidence: medium.** The core phenomenon is well documented, and I read the abstracts of the sources above. I did not find a source for the exact majority-rule, 3-state, rewire-to-same combination. The claim that majority rule shifts the details rests on Carro et al. (links, not nodes) and on my own reasoning.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** This is conserved segregation driven by swaps that happen only at boundaries. It's the same family as zero-temperature Kawasaki dynamics, the Schelling segregation model and voter models with conserved densities. The rock-paper-scissors framing doesn't explain what you saw.

**Why the rock-paper-scissors framing is misleading.** The defining rule (and both CNT_GE members) only swaps cells. It never changes a cell's colour, so how much of each colour exists stays fixed. That means `g_n_types=3` and `g_type_entropy=1.0` are just the starting mix carried forward. They are not emergent. In the 2D mobility model of Reichenbach, Mobilia and Frey, the patterns come from colour replacement, and the dynamics give a critical threshold of motility above which biodiversity is lost, but below which an entanglement of travelling spiral waves emerges. A related 1D/4-species paper shows that spiral formation takes place only without a conservation law for the total density. Your rule conserves colour counts, so you shouldn't expect spirals or species dying out. You see neither, so the first pass's analogy was the wrong one.

**What the rule actually does.** With 3 colours in a cycle, any two different colours are always "next" to each other one way or the other. So every boundary between colours has at least one cell allowed to move, while cells inside a solid domain stay put. Moving cells swap with a random neighbour, with no check on whether the swap helps. That is Schelling-style "unhappy agents move" dynamics. A related precedent: the zero temperature Ising model with infinite range Kawasaki dynamics evolves via exchanges of spins of opposite signs belonging to domain walls... equivalent to the Shelling's segregation model. Coarsening under conserved, local swaps is textbook. In the conserved Kawasaki dynamics... one finds n=1/3, and the additional conservation law makes domains grow significantly slower. Voter-type models with local conservation, explicitly motivated by Schelling, have also been studied (phase separation dynamics in models of the voter type, but with local conservation of the order parameter. Similar to the celebrated Schelling model). The kC=2 CNT_GE member is plain Schelling: a cell moves when at least 5 of its neighbours are colour 0.

**Why the fingerprint looks "non-textbook".** The small correlation length (about 6), the moderate Moran's I (0.63), about 6 domains and the reversals are what you'd expect from slow conserved coarsening seen at a finite time. The random, unconditional partner choice also roughens the boundaries; similar rough-boundary delays have been reported for Schelling variants (rougher interfaces, causing such delay). None of this is new behaviour.

**Artifact concerns.**
- The three CYCLE members with threshold 7 or 8 almost never meet the cycling condition, and with p=0.1 they rarely act even when they do. They are effectively pure p=1 swapping.
- I'm assuming SWAP means an unconditional random-neighbour exchange; I didn't verify the grammar. If that's right, those members are close to a random mixing walk. Then the small "domains" would just be finite-time or finite-lattice clumps, not real coarsening.
- So the 15-program class probably mixes real interface-gated segregation with near-trivial members. Before counting this as one behaviour, check each member's domain-size growth against time (L(t)).
- The colour diversity numbers are guaranteed by conservation and say nothing.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** This is the Schelling segregation model with vacancies, in the "unconstrained" form, with three agent classes.

**1. Model family.** Each cell is empty or holds an agent of class C. The classes are probably the three types, which fits `g_n_types=3` and `g_type_entropy=1.0`. The rule says that if the fraction of like neighbours is below θ (0.5 or 0.3), the agent moves to an empty cell. That is Schelling's threshold-and-relocate rule.
- The p=1.0 versus p=0.1 variants only change the update rate. They slow the dynamics and don't change the rule.
- The `kC=3` and `kC=4` variants most likely change the number of classes. I couldn't confirm that from the notation. It is also possible that kC sets something else, such as a neighbourhood or count parameter, so treat that reading as an assumption.
- The moving agent is not required to land somewhere it will be satisfied. That is the "unconstrained" Schelling variant, as in Mesa's Schelling example: unhappy agents pick a random empty cell to move to each step, until they are happy.

**2. Specific behaviour: coarsening and segregation with vacancies.**
- **Statistical-physics treatment.** Dall'Asta, Castellano and Marsili (arXiv 0707.1681) studied this model. In the unconstrained version, a clear coarsening process with the typical length of clusters growing as t^{1/z} with z=2 is observed for small ρ0. They also found that the coarsening process is robust against the variation of f* in a wide range around 1/2. Both findings match your run: it passes the domain-coarsening test and its threshold is 0.5.
- **Other studies.** The Aging-Schelling paper (Nature Sci. Rep. 2022) says the average interface density follows a power-law decay with an exponent α≃0.5 for the limit of small vacancy density, in agreement with the value reported for close variants of the Schelling model. The same paper sets out the frozen, segregated and mixed phases and a taxonomy of constrained versus unconstrained dynamics. It cites Domic, Goles and Rica, "Dynamics and complexity of the Schelling segregation model". I saw only the reference line for that paper and did not read it.
- **Phase diagram.** The Phase diagram of a Schelling segregation model (arXiv 0903.4694) describes clusters becoming more compact and well separated, with a process strongly reminiscent of coarsening in alloys.
- **Earliest source.** Schelling's own papers (1969 and 1971) are the origin. I did not confirm those citations in the search results, so I'm giving them from memory. The earliest source I verified is Dall'Asta et al. (2008).
- **Review.** The Sci. Rep. 2022 paper's introduction works as a short review of the statistical-physics literature. It notes the link to kinetic Ising-like models and to clustering and domain growth phenomena.

**3. Why the fingerprint may look non-textbook (a likely explanation, not a documented one).**
- **Three classes.** With three classes, a 0.5 like-neighbour threshold is harder to satisfy, and domains can jam as a multi-domain state. That would explain `g_n_domains≈3.9`. Three-group versions exist, for example the Schelling demo with up to three agent types, but I found no coarsening-exponent study for three types. Multi-type Schelling is a known variant, but its quantitative scaling here is not documented. I expect the same mechanism and a different exponent or prefactor.
- **Negative activity trend.** The falling activity (`g_activity_trend=-6.5`) is the usual approach to a quasi-frozen state, as unhappy agents run out. Dall'Asta et al. report a frozen or trapped disordered state at extreme intolerance, and the Sci. Rep. paper reports a frozen phase at low tolerance.
- **Slower p=0.1 runs.** These likely give a longer time to reach the same state.

I did not find a source describing the exact fingerprint of strong Moran's I together with a long correlation length, three domains and falling activity. I read that as a finite-size or finite-time view of ordinary coarsening, not a new phenomenon.

**4. Confidence: medium-high.** The model identification and the segregation-with-coarsening behaviour are well supported by sources I read. The remaining uncertainty is the exact meaning of `kC` and `MOVE_EMPTY`. For example, if the move is local rather than global, the exponent could change from the global-move case. That would still be a variant of the same known model.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** This is the Schelling segregation model on a lattice with vacancies, using blind random relocation. The three-colour version is a small variant, and I don't expect it to change the behaviour.

**1. Model family.** The system is a lattice of agents of kC=3 types plus empty sites. I read the primary rule as follows: an agent whose fraction of same-type neighbours is below 0.3 (`SAME_LT`, radius 1) jumps to a vacant site with probability 0.1. That is a Schelling-class relocation model, and every rule listed under "same class" is a threshold-triggered, probabilistic move to a vacant site.

**2. The behaviour in the literature.**
- **Earliest source.** Schelling (1969, 1971) is the origin. I did not retrieve either paper. I only saw secondary descriptions of them:
  - Schelling (1971) presented a two-dimensional version in which empty cells serve as destinations for relocating agents.
  - Schelling observed that this system always reached a segregated state with large same-colour clusters.
- **Physics-style treatment.** Gauvin, Vannimenus & Nadal, EPJ B 70, 293 (2009), arXiv:0903.4694, is the closest direct match:
  - Some sites are blank and agents of both colours may move to these vacancies.
  - Their phase diagram has a frozen state at low tolerance, a segregated state, and a mixed state at higher tolerance.
  - They also link the model to spin-1 models.
- **Reviews.**
  - Stauffer & Solomon (arXiv:0706.3983, a review-style paper) cover Schelling segregation and its relation to Ising and Potts models. They describe simulations with two and more groups.
  - The unified framework of arXiv:1104.1971 says the literature on the model's variants is fragmented.
- **Probabilistic, blind moves.** The "p=0.1 per step, move to a random vacancy" feature is standard:
  - Moves are "blind": the agent goes to a uniformly random vacant site.
  - In another formulation, any agent below the satisfaction threshold relocates at random to a vacant location.
  - Jones's variant added randomness and produced really large ghettos. I read Stauffer & Solomon as saying this randomness removes the blocking of cluster growth.
- **Three groups.** The three-colour case has also been studied. Fossett considered three residential groups (White, Black and Hispanic). I only saw a snippet of this source.

**3. What differs, and whether it matters.**
- **Three types instead of two.** The multi-group case is documented, so this is not new. With three types, a run could end in more than three domains. The Stauffer & Solomon review notes that with conserved group membership there is one domain per group at low-temperature equilibrium. **Verdict: KNOWN.** The model is a cyclic cellular automaton, or equivalently a cyclic particle system. The unusual fingerprint most likely comes from the stochastic update and from the system being observed before it has coarsened. It does not point to a new behaviour.

**1. Model family**
- The core rule is a 4-state cyclic CA with threshold 1. A cell advances from k to k+1 mod 4 if at least one neighbour is already in state k+1.
- The only change is that the advance happens with probability 0.1 per step. That makes it a probabilistic or asynchronous cyclic CA. It is also a discrete-time stand-in for the continuous-time cyclic particle system.
- The same-class members add extras to this core. These are Kuramoto phase coupling (K=1.0 and 0.1) and a two-field diffusive layer (CF, D=0.2/0.05).

**2. Is the behaviour reported?**
- **Earliest source for the deterministic rule.** Fisch, Gravner and Griffeath, "Cyclic Cellular Automata in Two Dimensions" (1991, *Spatial Stochastic Processes*). The chapter covers 2D cyclic CA and cyclic particle systems started from random states. After an initial metastable period of wave droplet formation and growth, the dynamic settles into a stable statistical equilibrium of large-scale spiralling wave formations. The Springer record lists "Spiral Formation" as a keyword. The abstract describes the dynamics of cyclic cellular automata.
- **Companion paper.** Fisch, Gravner and Griffeath, "Threshold-range scaling of excitable cellular automata" (*Statistics and Computing* 1, 23–39, 1991). They studied the ergodic behavior of these models on Z², started from random initial states.
- **Review-level descriptions.**
  - Wikipedia's cyclic CA entry says one-dimensional cyclic CA can be seen as interacting particle systems, while higher-dimensional ones show complex spiralling behaviour.
  - Tomlinson (2019) describes debris, then droplets, then defects, then spirals. Defects form where droplets meet and then give rise to spirals.
  - The stage sequence of debris, droplets and defects is the early phase of the deterministic CA.
- **Nearest stochastic and ecological relatives.**
  - Cyclic Lotka–Volterra and "rock-paper-scissors" lattice models are the stochastic-update analogue. Their spatial versions show spiral patterns.
  - The four-species cyclic case is studied in Roman, Konrad and Pleimling, "Cyclic competition of four species: domains and interfaces" (J. Stat. Mech. 2012, arXiv:1205.4914). It studies domain growth and interface fluctuations in 1D and 2D lattices of four cyclically interacting species.
  - Szabó and Sznaider (PRE 69, 031911, 2004) is an earlier 4-species lattice study. Above a vacancy threshold, symmetry-breaking order appears through growing domains containing only two neutral species.
  - Those 4-species models use different dynamics: exchange or mobility, empty sites, and predation rather than a threshold CA. They are a loose analogue only.
- **Stochastic excitable CAs.** A stochastic Greenberg–Hastings CA is studied in IJUC 7(1–2), 65–85 (2011). A continuous decrease in the excitation probability drives the system from an "active" to an "extinct" steady state.
- **Kuramoto-coupled and field-coupled extras.** I found no source on a Kuramoto-coupled or diffusive-field-coupled cyclic CA specifically. These extras are not needed for the observed behaviour, because the plain `C kC=4` rule already shows it.

**3. Why the fingerprint looks non-textbook**
- The standout features are 7.4 domains, 4 types with maximal type entropy, and high interface density. This is what you would expect from the early droplet, debris and defect stage, or from a system with many small spiral cores and domain walls.
- It would also fit a stochastic, small-p regime where waves are noisy.
- It does not fit the late-time picture of a few large, clean spirals.
- Small κ shrinks spirals. Spirals are much larger when the number of states is larger. With κ=4 and a noisy update, small, interface-rich spiral structure is expected.
- Threshold 1 is a special case. In a synchronous, deterministic CA with range 1, T=1 "quenches" incoherent local oscillations in that source's setup, so T=1 is a marginal case for clean spirals.
- Adding the p=0.1 asynchrony would plausibly change this. I did not find a source that studies exactly that route, so this is my inference.

**4. Caveats and confidence**
- I did not find a paper reporting κ=4, θ=1, per-cell probability 0.1 in this exact form.
- I also could not read the full text of Fisch et al. to check what it says about κ=4 specifically.
- The p-update is the standard probabilistic or asynchronous modification, and its spiral and domain behaviour is the same family of phenomena. That is why I call it KNOWN rather than KNOWN-VARIANT. Whether p=0.1 changes quantitative details such as domain counts or coarsening rate is not settled by these sources.
- Confidence is **medium-high**: the general behaviour is well documented, and the exact parameterisation is not.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** What was observed is ordinary cyclic-dominance domain coarsening. I found no twist in the behaviour itself that the literature doesn't already cover. The first pass's "KNOWN-VARIANT" rested on the exact update rule being undocumented, and an unusual rule doesn't count as a discovery.

**Why it's known**

- **The main rule is a cyclic CA with a voter-style step.** A cell is triggered by any neighbour in its successor state, then copies a random neighbour instead of the successor. The textbook rule is that each cell remains unchanged until some neighboring cell has a modular value exactly one unit larger than that of the cell itself, at which point it copies its neighbor's value. Copying a random neighbour weakens that cycle push and adds voter-like smoothing. Both of those lead towards coarsening rather than lasting spirals.
- **Four states that persist while domains grow is the standard result for N=4.** For cyclic Lotka-Volterra systems, the arising spatial patterns form a mosaic of single-species domains with algebraically growing size, ℓ(t)∼t^α, where α=3/4 (1/2) and 1/3 for N=3 with sequential (parallel) dynamics and N=4. For N<5 ... single-species domains arise and grow indefinitely, and the process exhibits coarsening. With 4 species, there appear static interfaces denoted by S (AC, BD, CA, and DB), in addition to the previously defined right moving interfaces. Pairs of states that don't interact (0–2 and 1–3) form borders that stay put. That explains all three readings together: 4 types surviving, falling activity (−1.03), and a Moran's I of only 0.595 rather than near 1. That 1996 analysis is 1-D; the general rule that fixation depends on the number of species versus the dimension, and that moving invasion fronts otherwise maintain a self-organizing polydomain structure, is also documented.
- **The 3-state variants with stochastic CYCLE(th=2) fall within the documented threshold behaviour of cyclic CAs.** The CCA has three generic forms of long-term behavior, depending on the size of the threshold relative to the range. Possible outcomes include static blocks, periodic spirals and an intermediate range of thresholds where incoherent traveling waves form, propagate for a while, and then disperse. Mixing in COPY or MAJ steps only adds known voter or majority coarsening. I haven't checked where exactly each 3-state variant falls in that range.
- **Not looking like textbook spirals is expected.** Spirals win only when the push around the cycle is strong. Here random copying dilutes it, so you get the coarsening and dying-down regime instead of a lattice taken over by spirals.

**Real pattern or artifact?** It's a real emergent pattern (domain growth with interfaces), not a numerical artifact. It is generic, though: 27 different rule programs land on it, which is what you'd expect from a common attractor. One caution: the falling activity suggests the runs may be heading to a frozen state with non-interacting neighbours. So the measured domain counts and correlation length could just be a snapshot partway through coarsening. That's a measurement-timing issue, not new behaviour.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** I'm downgrading the first pass's KNOWN-VARIANT. The first pass found a new rule, not a new behaviour. Every observed feature (cyclic switching, oscillation, then consensus) is already described for three-state cyclic-dominance systems on graphs.

**What the rule is.** A node changes only when a neighbour holds its successor state, as in a cyclic cellular automaton. But it copies a random neighbour rather than the successor, so it's a voter model gated by cyclic dominance. The other programs in this class mix pure copying (voter) with pure successor-stepping (cyclic automaton), so the whole class sits between two well-studied models.

**Each feature against the literature:**
- **Cyclic dynamics and fixation in this 3-state setting.** Bramson & Griffeath, "Flux and fixation in cyclic particle systems" (1989), is the standard reference, and the cyclic cellular automaton was proposed by Bramson and Griffeath as the deterministic counterpart of the cyclic particle system. For 3 or 4 colours the 1-D systems cluster, meaning that contiguous regions of all one type grow arbitrarily large. That clustering is the mechanism behind consensus on a finite network.
- **Voter copying combined with cyclic dominance.** This exact hybrid has been studied: Szabó & Szolnoki, "A three-state cyclic voter model extended with Potts energy" (Phys. Rev. E 65, 036115, 2002).
- **Oscillation followed by absorbing consensus on networks.** In the rock-paper-scissors model on small-world networks, the amplitude of oscillation increases with the measure of randomness and the increasing oscillation terminates at one of the absorbing (homogeneous) states. That is the same route as here: oscillation, then cyclic changes, then consensus.
- **Oscillation, consensus and fragmentation in cyclic opinion models.** Demirel et al. report stationary phase, oscillatory phase, consensus phase, and fragmented phase regimes.

**Is it a real pattern or trivial?** The consensus is real but generic. On a finite graph, any copy-based dynamics eventually reaches an absorbing single-state configuration, and the cyclic gate mostly changes how fast. The odd fingerprint is probably explained by the setup rather than new behaviour:
- The rule changes node states only, never edges, so `n_components`, `n_giant` and `n_degree_cv` most likely describe the fixed network rather than anything the dynamics did.
- The modest oscillation and cyclic-change scores are the expected transient before absorption.
- The fact that 89 programs converge on this fingerprint suggests a broad, generic attractor, not a fine-tuned effect.

One caveat: I didn't find a paper on this exact gated-copy rule (copy a random neighbour only when a successor neighbour exists, at p=0.1). But the rule combination isn't the question, and its behaviour is covered by the work above.

text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** The core rule is the voter model on a sparse network. The REWIRE variant is the coevolving (adaptive) voter model. My confidence is medium-high for the core rule and medium for the Kuramoto and CYCLE hybrids.

**1. Model family**
- `N kN=4 | ALWAYS -> COPY_RAND p=0.2` means each node, with probability 0.2, copies the state of a randomly chosen neighbour in a degree-~4 graph. That is the standard pull voter model. My search turned up this description: an individual "imports" its state from a randomly chosen neighbor.
- `N.REWIRE(p=0.003); N.COPY(p=0.3)` is copying plus slow link rewiring. That is the coevolving voter model: The coevolving voter model consists of two dynamical processes: copying and rewiring.
- `N.KURA(K); N.COPY(p)` and `N.CYCLE; N.COPY(p=1.0)` are hybrids of a phase-oscillator step with voter copying. I did not find a canonical model for these. The closest related work I found treats consensus as synchronisation in a Kuramoto-type opinion model (consensus as a peculiar kind of synchronization (frequency locking)). That is a conceptual link, not the same system.

**2. The specific behaviours**
- **Consensus (n_giant, n_consensus_gain).** Voter dynamics on finite connected graphs reach consensus. One source states that the voter algorithm converges to a network wide consensus in finite networks. Consensus time depends on network structure: the average time TN to reach consensus for a network of N nodes with an uncorrelated degree distribution scales as N mu1 2/mu2. This is from Sood, Antal & Redner, PRE 77, 041121 (2008), "Voter models on heterogeneous networks".
- **Duality with coalescing random walks.** The duality relationship between voter models and "coalescing RWs" makes analysis of RWs a powerful approach for calculating consensus probability and mean consensus time. This is in the review "Random walks and diffusion on networks" (arXiv:1612.03281).
- **Multiple components, with a giant component alongside them (n_components).** This is the fragmentation behaviour of rewiring voter models. Holme & Newman (PRE 74, 056108, 2006) found a transition between a giant community and many small ones, and Durrett et al. describe it: When α = 1, only rewiring steps occur, so once all of the M edges have been touched, the graph has been disconnected into G components.
  - Vazquez, Eguíluz & San Miguel (PRL 100, 108702, 2008) identified a "generic absorbing transition" with an active phase and a frozen phase.
  - With rewiring this slow (p=0.003 against copying at 0.3), I would expect consensus before fragmentation. I did not test that.
- **Review sources.**
  - Adaptive voter models: "Modeling complex systems with adaptive networks" (arXiv:1301.2561) says The simplest and best-understood model exhibiting the fragmentation transition is the adaptive voter model.
  - Coevolving voter models: arXiv:2311.05882 / Frontiers in Complex Systems 2023 is a review of coevolving nonlinear voter models.
- **Oscillation (n_oscillation, 0.808).** I did not find a source for oscillation in plain voter dynamics. It is probably finite-size fluctuation of the state densities, or a metric artefact. In the KURA variants the oscillation is probably just the Kuramoto phases. I could not verify this, and it is the weakest part of my conclusion.

**3. Why the fingerprint looks atypical**
The test passes (consensus gain is high), but the profile differs from textbook voter-model output. That is expected for two reasons. The 49 programs mix several mechanisms, and a metric suite designed for other behaviours will pick up side effects such as component counts and degree variation. A mixed profile does not on its own indicate a new phenomenon.

**Caveats**
- The earliest clear source is Clifford & Sudbury (1973) and Holley & Liggett (1975), cited from memory. My searches did not return those papers, so I have not verified them. The earliest sources I verified are Holme & Newman 2006 and Vazquez et al. 2008, which I saw only in the reference lists of the papers above.
- I did not find a source for the exact Kuramoto-plus-copy and cycle-plus-copy hybrids. If those are the interesting part, they could be KNOWN-VARIANT or LITERATURE-SILENT. I did not run a dedicated search for them, so I cannot call them literature-silent.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** I'm downgrading the first pass's KNOWN-VARIANT. The run shows cooperators and defectors coexisting in a small number of smoothed-out clusters on a lattice where agents imitate the best-scoring neighbour. That is a known effect of adding conformity (copying the local majority) to the spatial Prisoner's Dilemma. I found no feature that needs a new behavioural explanation.

**Base behaviour.** In Nowak & May's model, every agent plays itself and its 8 neighbours, then all agents update at once by copying the best-scoring cell in that group, choosing at random between ties. The result is cooperators and defectors coexisting, with clusters of both types of players expanding, colliding and fragmenting. Your class contains this exact setup: the members with payoffs (1.9, 0) are almost exactly Nowak & May's chaotic setting, DC-payoff = 1.85 with CD = DD = 0.

**Why the fingerprint isn't textbook.** The step where each cell copies its neighbourhood majority with probability 0.1 is a conformity rule. Mixing majority-copying with payoff-driven copying is well studied:
- Szolnoki & Perc found that spatial selection for cooperation is enhanced if an appropriate fraction of the population chooses the most common rather than the most profitable strategy.
- They also showed that conformists can form an efficient surface around cooperative clusters and guarantee smooth interfaces between diverse strategy domains.
- Later work reports conformity induces within-cluster behavioral homogeneity and between-cluster behavioral diversity.
- More generally, some works have considered the mixed rule in combination with the payoff-driven and conformity-driven strategy update procedures, and in some of them cooperators can survive with defectors under the mixed update rule.

The observed features fit this. About 3.6 domains means fewer, smoother clusters than pure Nowak–May chaos produces. A type entropy of 0.83 (roughly a 25/75 split) means stable coexistence. That explains why the run passes the spatial-chaos test but doesn't look like textbook spatial chaos.

**Differences from the literature, all at the rule level rather than in the behaviour:**
- **Payoffs:** S = −0.5 is a strict Prisoner's Dilemma, not the "weak" version with S = 0.
- **Update scheme:** everyone updates at once by copying the best scorer; Szolnoki & Perc updated one random cell at a time with a probabilistic (Fermi) rule.
- **Who conforms:** every cell conforms with probability 0.1 each step, rather than a fixed subgroup of conformists.

As you said, an undocumented rule combination isn't a discovery. The behaviour is the same.

**Is it a real pattern or an artifact?** It's a real emergent pattern, but a generic one. "2 types" only says that both strategies survived. The rising activity and single trend reversal are thin evidence: they could be a slow transient on a small 64×64 grid. I can't verify that from summary statistics alone. One oddity: about 3.6 domains alongside a correlation length of only 2.3 is a bit inconsistent. It may come from how these metrics are normalised rather than from the dynamics. Neither point is a sign of new phenomenology.

**What's actually driving the pattern.** Rule (1) is a plain voter model: the multi-state voter model (VM) is one of the most studied models of non-equilibrium statistical physics. In the main program it runs on every cell, every step, so it dominates. The movement rule just adds a bit of extra mixing on top. As I read the rule text, the empty state (type 0) gets copied like any other type. So in practice this is a 4-state voter model where "empty" is one of the opinions. Empty cells aren't conserved, which means the "vacancies" here aren't really vacancies in the Schelling sense.

**Why the fingerprint fits voter coarsening, not textbook Schelling.**
- **Many domains (6.7), 3–4 of the 4 types still present, short correlation length, high interface density.** This is what a 2D voter model looks like partway through. It does coarsen toward a single domain, but very slowly: the density of active interfaces vanishes only as 1/ln(t/τ). On a 64×64 grid you'd expect to catch several domains with most types still surviving.
- **Ragged rather than compact domains.** Voter dynamics is driven solely by interfacial noise, and domains keep their fractal geometry at all scales even late in the dynamics. That's why the run passes a segregation test but doesn't look like classic Schelling, which forms compact blocks.
- **Combining Schelling and voter dynamics is itself published.** In the Schelling–Voter model, unhappy agents can not only move elsewhere but also adapt to a new state. The differences here (everyone copies, not just unhappy agents; 4 types; updates happen all at once) don't create a new kind of behaviour. They just push the system further toward the voter end.
- **Possible open detail, unchecked.** Multi-state voter models can coarsen algebraically, and adding intermediate states restores an effective surface tension. Your measurements are from a single moment, so I can't tell which growth law applies. That would be a question for a time-series measurement, not something visible in the current fingerprint.

**Real pattern or artifact?** The pattern is real, but it's ordinary, well-documented voter coarsening caught before it finishes. The "segregation with vacancies" label is partly an artifact: the empty state is just one more copied type, and the movement threshold matters little. That would explain why 123 programs, including the order-swapped and p=0.1 versions, land in the same class. The p=0.1 versions are the weakest point of this argument. **Verdict: KNOWN, with medium confidence.** One part is only partly covered: the cyclic-threshold rule run on a random graph with copy noise. I found no paper that studies that exact combination.

**1. Model family**
- Rule (1) is a threshold cyclic cellular automaton (Griffeath's CCA), run on a sparse random graph instead of a lattice. A cell of colour k changes to k+1 mod κ if at least T cells of that colour are in its neighbourhood. Here κ=4 and T=3.
- Rule (2) is voter-model copying. Applied alone it is the noisy voter model, also called the Kirman model.
- The sibling programs in the class are the same family. COPY;COPY and MAJ;MAJ are voter or majority dynamics with noise. COPY;KURA is a copy rule with a Kuramoto-style coupling, which I did not search for.

**2. The specific behaviour: consensus in a copy-noise system on a random graph**
- **Earliest source I could verify:** the voter model goes back to Clifford & Sudbury (1973), "A model for spatial conflict", Biometrika 60, 581. I only saw this in a reference list, not the paper itself. Clifford and Sudbury's paper appears there as reference [5].
- **Main source on networks:** Carro, Toral & San Miguel (2016), "The noisy voter model on complex networks", Sci. Rep. 6:24775. It describes the competition between copying and noise. It produces a noise-induced, finite-size transition between a mostly ordered regime and a mostly disordered one. This transition has also been reported on network topologies for both the Kirman model and the noisy voter model. The same paper covers Erdős–Rényi graphs.
- **Why consensus appears:** Without noise, the voter model has absorbing states of full order. Noise at p=0.1 or 0.03 on N=200 gives intermittent or transient consensus. That is the finite-size bimodal/unimodal behaviour in Carro et al. It explains why the COPY;COPY and MAJ;MAJ programs show "consensus".
- **Components and giant component:** the large n_components and n_giant values are almost certainly a property of the graph, not the dynamics. A mean degree of 4 gives a giant component of about 98% and a few small isolated pieces. Each isolated piece can reach consensus separately, so the global fingerprint looks unlike a textbook single-network consensus run. This is my inference. I did not search for a source on it.

**3. The cyclic part of the rule**
- Griffeath's CCA is well documented on lattices. The behaviour depends on threshold relative to range. High thresholds give static blocks of solid colour. Very low thresholds give global oscillation, sometimes as spiral waves. Intermediate thresholds give "turbulence".
- Early sources: Fisch, Gravner & Griffeath, "Threshold-range scaling of excitable cellular automata", Statistics and Computing 1 (1991), and the 2D chapter in Spatial Stochastic Processes (1991). I only saw these cited. Shalizi et al., arXiv nlin/0507067, is a readable review.
- The CCA site also describes a "cyclic turbulence" phase that needs large arrays. It notes that small systems inevitably fixate. A 200-node graph is small, so fixation is expected.
- On a degree-4 graph with threshold 3, a node needs three of its roughly four neighbours to be one type ahead. Cycling is therefore local and short-lived. In my reading, copy noise supplies the consensus and the cycle rule supplies only transient oscillation. The n_oscillation score is consistent with that.

**4. Cyclic dominance on random graphs (related, not identical)**
- Rock-paper-scissors dynamics on random and complex networks are well studied. Global oscillations can emerge when the interaction network has small-world properties. On random graphs, one species often goes extinct early.
- These are invasion-rate models, not threshold-CCA models, so they are only a rough analogue.

**5. Why not LITERATURE-SILENT, and what remains uncertain**
- For the consensus finding, the voter-model and noisy-voter literature covers it directly.
- For the exact system (threshold CCA with p-copy noise on an ER graph, N=200), I found no direct paper. That is the part where a KNOWN-VARIANT label could be argued. I judge the difference unlikely to matter. Consensus is driven by the voter component, and the CCA part adds only short-lived local cycling.
- My searches may have missed niche papers on "cyclic CA on networks".

**Verdict: KNOWN.** The behaviour here, consensus on one connected network while rewiring is slow, is the textbook result for networks where opinions and links change together. It's also close to trivial: at this rewiring rate the game decides the outcome almost by itself.

**Why this is known behaviour**

- **Opinion side.** Holme and Newman's model has two processes, copying a neighbour or rewiring to someone who agrees. When rewiring is the weaker process, "a giant community of like-minded individuals forms." At average degree 4, the switch happens at a critical parameter value φ_c ≈ 0.458. A 0.01 rewiring chance is far below that.
- **Your exact rewiring rule is covered.** Your rule (cut a link to a different-type neighbour, reconnect to a random same-type node) is the "rewire-to-same" model of Durrett et al. (PNAS). They report this rewire-to-same model has a phase transition similar to that of Holme and Newman.
- **Game side.** Zimmermann, Eguíluz and San Miguel studied the same setup: each agent plays a Prisoner's Dilemma game with its local neighbors, collects an aggregate payoff, and imitates the strategy of its best neighbor. They found the system typically reaches either a full-defective state or a highly cooperative steady state. One of their two outcomes is a single-strategy state, which is what you see.
- **The only real difference.** In their model, a cut link goes to another randomly chosen agent, whereas yours goes to a same-type node. That changes the rules, not the observed behaviour. With p=0.01, very few links get rewired before the whole network has adopted one strategy, so the target rule hardly matters.

**Do the features reflect a real pattern or an artifact?** Mostly the expected result of the game dominating, not a new route to consensus.
- **Single component (n_giant ≈ 1, n_components high):** a 200-node random network with average degree 4 starts with a giant component. Rewiring is too slow to split it before consensus.
- **Oscillation (0.57):** probably the usual flip-flopping of everyone updating at once under best-neighbour copying during the early phase, before one strategy takes over.
- **Edge turnover and degree spread (~0.55):** these come from the few rewirings during that early phase. After consensus there are no different-type links left, so rewiring stops completely. This differs from Holme–Newman, where edges keep being rearranged within groups after consensus . That difference follows directly from your rule, so it isn't new behaviour.
- **Type entropy (0.35):** a moderate value is consistent with a mostly one-type end state.
- **Why it doesn't look like textbook consensus:** consensus here comes from payoff-driven copying (probably defection sweeping the network at T=1.9), not from the usual voter-model drift. That route is itself documented in the Zimmermann line of work.

**Caveat:** I don't know which strategy wins, or whether the run reaches full consensus or stops at a near-absorbing mixed state. If a stable mostly-cooperative state with leader nodes appeared instead, that would be the separate, also documented Zimmermann outcome. If the oscillation persists after consensus, that would not fit this explanation and would be worth a closer look.

**Why I disagree with the first pass**

- **The payoff puts it in a known frozen regime.** If g=(1.5, 0.5) gives a temptation of about b=1.5, the rule sits in Nowak–May's 1<b<1.8 band. The chaotic regime only applies for 1.8 < b < 2, cooperators and defectors coexist indefinitely in a chaotically shifting balance. Below 1.8, the cluster rules are: (b < 1.8) big D cluster will shrink; (b < 2) 2x2 or larger cluster of C will continue to grow. In that regime equilibrium frequency of cooperators depends upon the initial conditions.
- **The fingerprint matches that regime.** One domain covers about 90% of the grid (largest_domain 0.897). There are about 4 domains in total, a correlation length of 2, one reversal and moderate clustering (Moran's I 0.5). That is one type taking over, with a few small leftover islands of the other type that stop changing. Real Nowak–May chaos looks different: the cooperator fraction hovers around 0.318, with clusters of both types of players expanding, colliding and fragmenting.
- **The "chaos" label is probably a false positive.** A single reversal followed by a 90% majority is not chaos. The "domain coarsening" label fits better, but it is coarsening that stops early and freezes.
- **The other rule programs in the class change nothing important.** The COPY versions add small random copying, which works like mutation noise. The SWAP versions (p≈0.002–0.01) add random movement, which is a studied extension: the effects of an unconditional move rule in the spatial Prisoner's Dilemma, Snowdrift and Stag Hunt games have been examined, and Vainstein and Arenzon extended the original Nowak–May PDG model by considering a regular lattice where some sites are empty, which allows diffusion of individuals. At these low rates, movement just stirs the small leftover islands a little.
- **The count gate doesn't matter.** CNT_GE(th=3) only lets a cell update when enough neighbours meet a condition, which mostly freezes things further. The exact rule combination being unpublished is not a discovery.

**Trivial or emergent?** Low complexity, but not a pure artifact. It is a real, documented spatial-game outcome: local selection drives the grid to near-fixation and leaves small frozen islands. It is not sustained pattern formation. Whether it reads as Prisoner's Dilemma or snowdrift depends on how (1.5, 0.5) maps onto the payoffs, which I couldn't confirm. Both versions are well documented, so the verdict holds either way.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** I don't think this is even a variant. What you observed matches a well-documented result: the "spatial chaos" of Nowak-May disappears when not every cell updates at once, and the lattice settles into a few still blocks of one strategy.

**Why the first pass was too generous**

1. **The base rule is Nowak-May at its chaotic setting.** In the original model each cell copies the neighbour with the highest score, which at b≈1.9 produces complex and persistent spatial patterns, allowing cooperators and defectors to coexist through the constant formation and breakup of clusters.
2. **Updating only 10–30% of cells per step is a studied scheme, not a new twist.** Huberman & Glance (1993) found that with one-cell-at-a-time updating, the matrix converges rapidly to steady-state and does not display the widely changing spatial patterns observed in the synchronous case. Nowak, Bonhoeffer & May (1994) agreed that the interesting behavior for 1.8 < b < 2 in the deterministic game has disappeared, though cooperators and defectors still coexist. The in-between case, where a fraction p of agents update each step, has its own paper: a detailed study of more realistic system of semi-synchronous updates where pN agents are updated at every time instant, which reports a first-order phase transition.
3. **Your fingerprint is what those papers describe:** only 2 strategies left, about 4 domains, a correlation length of 2, activity falling over time, and a single reversal. That is a lattice slowing down into a few fixed blocks, not textbook chaos. In the extreme case the lattice ends up as a single static solid slab of one color. Your runs look like they stopped just short of that, in the coexistence state Nowak, Bonhoeffer & May describe.
4. **The neighbour-count gate (CNT_LE / CNT_GE) has no exact match in the literature, but it doesn't change the behaviour.** It just thins out further which cells can update, which acts like another form of asynchrony. The other rules in the same class reach the same frozen-block result by different routes: majority voting plus a game, or several games plus rare copying. That a mix of mechanisms coarsens into domains is also well known. Under your own criterion, a new rule combination that produces known behaviour is not a discovery.

**Real pattern or artifact?** The domains themselves are real emergent clusters. But the "chaos" label looks like a misclassification: either the test is picking up the early transient before things settle, or it is reacting to random update noise. The overall result is a near-frozen, almost trivial end state. So I've marked it as trivial/artifact, meaning the chaos classification, not the clusters.

**Nothing left unexplained**, as far as I can find.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** The system is the Vicsek model, and the dense clustered flocking state it produced is well documented.

**1. Model family.** `HEAD_MEAN(b=any, r=0.5)` with speed v and noise η is the standard Vicsek model. Each particle moves at constant speed. At each step it takes the mean heading of neighbours within radius r and adds angular noise. The original paper describes it this way: particles are driven with a constant absolute velocity and at each time step assume the average direction of motion of the particles in their neighborhood with some random perturbation (η) added.

The "same class" variants (`ATTRACT` plus `ALIGN`) add cohesion, which is the Grégoire–Chaté cohesive Vicsek family.

**2. The specific behaviour.** Your run shows high polar order (0.84) and high local alignment (0.89). It also shows very strong density heterogeneity (density CV 6.2) and a low nearest-neighbour ratio (0.18), meaning strong clustering. That points to a Vicsek system in its phase-separated or clustered ordered regime, not a homogeneous flock. This is the established picture:

- **Earliest source for the model.** Vicsek, Czirók, Ben-Jacob, Cohen and Shochet, PRL 75, 1226 (1995). It reports a kinetic phase transition from no transport to finite net transport through spontaneous symmetry breaking.
- **Earliest clear source for the density structure.** Grégoire & Chaté, PRL 92, 025702 (2004). They found the transition is always discontinuous, including for the minimal model of Vicsek et al. Chaté, Ginelli, Grégoire and Raynaud, PRE 77, 046113 (2008) then showed that well-defined high-density and high-order propagating solitary structures dominate the dynamics over a large part of parameter space. They add that these bands are dynamical objects made of splitting and merging clusters. The arXiv version is 0712.2062.
- **Clustering and intermittency.** Huepe & Aldana, PRL 92, 168701 (2004), is the earliest report of cluster statistics in this model. It describes particles aggregating into clusters that play an essential role in the intermittent dynamics. The 2008 paper above corrects part of their interpretation. It says clusters of size n are distributed algebraically in the ordered region, with an exponent that changes with distance to the transition.
- **Review.** Ginelli, "The Physics of the Vicsek model," EPJ ST 225, 2099 (2016), arXiv:1511.01451. It states that for the Vicsek class phase separation takes the form of high-density ordered bands that travel in a low-density sea of disordered particles. It also covers giant number fluctuations in the homogeneous ordered phase. A shorter essay-level review (Chatterjee, UCSD PHYS 563) says the same.
- **Cluster phases in the same system.** More recent work reports cluster phases and "flocking within clusters" as the interaction radius or noise changes (arXiv:2307.12538).

**3. What is different or unexplained.** The "doesn't look textbook" fingerprint is probably a matter of parameters, not new physics. I did not see the box size, density or particle count, so this is an inference. Low speed (v = 0.3) with r = 0.5 and low noise (η = 0.1) is the slow, low-noise corner where clustered or band-like states with strong density contrast are expected. In that corner the usual homogeneous polar flock is not what you would see.

Two features I could not match to specific literature:

- **Angular momentum (0.327).** This could come from rotating clusters or periodic-boundary effects. The delayed-Vicsek paper I found mentions swirls, but that is a different system, so I am not calling this documented.
- **Step statistic (5.995).** This is a measurement-specific quantity that I could not map to anything.

Both are minor next to the main behaviour. Neither suggests a new phenomenon without further analysis.

**4. Confidence: medium-high.** The model identification and the band/cluster phenomenology are firmly established, with primary sources and a review. I lowered it from "high" because I could not verify the simulation's density, box size or exact metric definitions. I also could not tie the angular-momentum signal to a specific source.

**Verdict: KNOWN.** I'm downgrading the first pass's KNOWN-VARIANT. What the run shows is ordinary clustering and coarsening in a threshold voter model with neighbour swapping added. I found no behaviour that isn't already described, and the fact that this exact rule combination wasn't found in print doesn't count as a discovery.

**1. What the rule is.** With only 2 types, the "cycle" rule just means: switch to the other type if at least 3 of your 8 neighbours already have it. That is the threshold voter model, which was introduced by Cox and Durrett and studied in depth by Liggett and others. In that model individuals update their opinion at rate one (continuous time) and change their opinion if and only if the number of opponents in their neighborhood is at least equal to τ. The known picture is that as the threshold τ increases from one to the neighborhood size, the system goes from a phase of coexistence to a phase of clustering to a phase of fixation. A threshold of 3 out of 8 sits between those extremes. Both ends of that sequence are proved: the threshold-1 case is known to cluster if N = d = 1 and coexists in every other case (Liggett 1994). For larger thresholds, Durrett and Steif proved fixation. Your observations fit the clustering-to-fixation part: a few large domains, falling activity, and no type taking over.

**2. The swapping.** Adding neighbour exchange on top of spin flips is the standard "stirring" setup. Durrett and Neuhauser studied it with stirring at a fast rate, i.e., for each x, y ... we exchange the values at x and y at rate e^-2. In physics it appears as Ising models whose time evolution occurs as a consequence of a combination of spin-flip (Glauber) and spin-exchange (Kawasaki) processes. That covers the same-class variants that use majority plus swap.

**3. A check I worked out myself (not from a source).** In the very-fast-swapping limit, neighboring sites become independent, so the system follows a simple average-density equation. For this rule (3 of 8 neighbours, two types) that equation has three stable states: all one type, all the other, and a 50/50 mix. So moderate swapping (1 swap step per 0.1 flip probability) could leave the grid with pure regions next to well-mixed regions, rather than two clean opposing phases. That would explain a "non-textbook" fingerprint. It is still covered by Durrett and Neuhauser's theory for systems with two competing stable states, where the outcome is decided by which way the boundary between them moves.

**4. Is it real or an artifact? Mostly real, but strongly affected by grid size.** The pattern genuinely emerges: ordered domains form from a random start. However:
- A correlation length of about 20 cells on a 64-cell grid, with about 4.6 domains, means the domains are already a third of the grid wide. Coarsening is probably close to stopping because of the grid's size, which by itself makes the fingerprint look unusual.
- At a threshold below the majority, the boundaries between domains wander like voter-model boundaries rather than smoothing out under surface tension. That gives slow, noisy coarsening.
- If the swap moves values in a fixed pattern rather than with random partners, it is close to a no-op for these statistics. In that case the run is just the threshold voter model.
- 29 rule programs landing in the same class fits this being a generic behaviour.

**Possible follow-ups:**
- Check whether the low-type regions are pure or mixed. Mixed regions would point to the three-state effect in point 3.
- Run larger grids to see whether the unusual fingerprint disappears.

**Verdict: KNOWN-VARIANT, leaning toward KNOWN.** The behaviour itself is documented. What hasn't been written up is this exact pairing of mechanisms, and that alone isn't a discovery.

**1. The cyclic step is a known, named rule.** Rule (2) with 3 types, the 8-cell neighbourhood and threshold 3 is Griffeath's "313" rule. The MCell rule list gives it as R1/T3/C3/NM and calls it "the only three-color rule in the range-1 CCA rulespace that exhibits significant self-organization." It belongs to the threshold–range cyclic automaton family, where a cell's color advances by 1 if there are at least Threshold cells of the next color in its neighbourhood. That family's phases are mapped out. At intermediate thresholds incoherent traveling waves form, propagate, collide and disperse (the "turbulent" phase). For larger neighbourhoods, a complex mix of color blocks and partial spirals, called turbulence, can form.

**2. Adding a random copying or swapping step is also covered.** Rule (1) is a voter-model step; the SWAP siblings are an exchange step. Both work like mobility in rock-paper-scissors models. In those models, a critical threshold of motility is identified, above which biodiversity is lost, but below which an entanglement of travelling spiral waves emerges. The authors say this is robust, it does not depend on the details of cyclic competition or spatial environment. The stochastic, continuous-time version of cyclic competition is Bramson & Griffeath's cyclic particle system. The deterministic automaton was proposed by Bramson and Griffeath as the deterministic counterpart of the cyclic particle system. So this hybrid sits between two well-studied relatives.

**3. Why the fingerprint isn't textbook.** A correlation length of about 4.7 cells on a 64×64 grid, a few domains, balanced types (entropy ≈ 1) and a high reversal rate (0.5) look like strongly noise-disrupted cyclic waves. Copying a random neighbour every step with p=1 is heavy noise, so cells near domain borders flip back and forth. That likely explains most of the high reversal score; it's probably not new dynamics. My reading is that this sits in the known "turbulent / noisy cyclic domains" regime, with the noise keeping spiral cores small and short-lived. I found nothing in the behaviour that the literature leaves unexplained. The only gap is that no paper simulates exactly 313 plus every-step synchronous voter copying.

**Genuine or artifact?** The cyclic wave activity is genuine: it passes the standard test, and the deterministic 313 core is known to self-organise. The odd parts of the fingerprint (small domains, high reversals) are best read as what the noise step does to known dynamics, not a new pattern. 45 rule programs landing in the same class is what you'd expect if they all share a cyclic step plus a mixing step.

**How to make this KNOWN outright:** run 313 with no copy step on the same 64×64 grid with the same metrics, then turn the copy probability down gradually. If you see a smooth crossover from spirals to small turbulent domains, this is the standard noise-versus-spiral-size trade-off.
